title: Handbook of Nature Study
sourceTitle: Handbook of Nature-Study for Teachers and Parents
author: Anna Botsford Comstock
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #78142: public domain in the USA; first published 1911 (Ithaca: Comstock Publishing Company), before 1930. Author Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930). Lessons link to the Gutenberg text; no text is reproduced.
description: Anna Botsford Comstock's 1911 classic is the nature-study bible of Charlotte Mason families: hundreds of short studies of birds, fish, insects, wild flowers, trees, rocks, weather and stars. Each sitting is an outdoor observation, a few minutes of the parent's background reading shared aloud, and a nature-journal sketch, so the whole family can do it together across grades 1–8. It's a public-domain classic, and the full text is free online.
includes: 249 lessons in 26 units, one per study in the book
Link to the exact study in the free full text for every lesson
An outdoor observation for each bird, animal, plant, rock or star
Observation questions, with answers where there is one right answer
Safety and 'what's changed since 1911' notes for the parent

units.title: Getting Started: The Teaching of Nature-Study (Part I)

lessons.title: What Nature-Study Is (for the parent)
steps: Parent reads the opening sections of Part I (pp. 1–7) about what nature-study should do for the child and the teacher
Take a slow, unhurried walk outside together with no goal except noticing
Give each child a blank notebook to be their nature journal; draw one thing from the walk

links.label: Read: Part I, The Teaching of Nature-Study (p. 1)

questions: What is one thing you noticed on the walk that you had never noticed before?
lessons.notes: Comstock says it is fine, even good, for a parent to say "I do not know; let us find out together."

lessons.title: The Field Note-book
steps: Parent reads "The Field Note-book" (pp. 13–14)
Go outside and choose one plant or creature to watch for ten minutes
Make the first real journal entry: a sketch, the date, the place and the weather
questions: What three things should every journal entry have besides your drawing?
answers: The date, the place and the weather (any reasonable answer)
lessons.notes: Comstock warns against forcing neat notebooks; the journal belongs to the child.

lessons.title: The Field Excursion and Pets as Nature-Study Subjects
steps: Parent reads "The Field Excursion" and "Pets as Nature-Study Subjects" (pp. 15–16)
Plan a short field trip with one clear thing to look for, then go
Nature journal: draw a map of where you went and mark what you found
questions: What did you set out to find on your field trip, and did you find it?
Which pet or animal at home could you study closely?

units.title: Unit 1: Bird Study I — Feathers, Flight and Farmyard Birds

lessons.title: Beginning Bird Study in the Primary Grades
steps: Outdoors: Visit a backyard flock or farm and watch a hen walk, peck, scratch and drink for ten minutes
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Beginning Bird Study in the Primary Grades" (p. 25) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch the hen from the side, labeling beak, comb, wattles and feet, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: Beginning Bird Study in the Primary Grades (p. 25)

questions: Why is the hen a good first bird to study?
What did the hen do most while you watched?
answers: She is easy to find and watch up close, and she is a real bird

lessons.title: Feathers as Clothing
steps: Nature walk: Find feathers on the ground or at a farm and look closely at how they lie on a bird's body; if it rains, notice how a hen looks standing in it
Parent previews the background reading on "Feathers as Clothing" (p. 27) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a body feather and a fluffy down feather side by side, and add the date and place
questions: Which part of a feather lies next to the bird's skin, the smooth web or the fluff?
What are feathers that are all fluff called?
How do feathers keep a bird dry and warm?
answers: The fluffy part
Down
The smooth outer parts shed water and the fluff underneath holds in warmth

lessons.title: Feathers as Ornament
steps: Go and look: Compare a rooster and a hen (or a drake and a duck) and note which one has the brighter, fancier feathers
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Feathers as Ornament" (p. 30) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw the rooster's curved tail feathers next to the hen's plainer tail; label what you can and date it
questions: Are the rooster's long curved tail feathers mainly for flying?
Why is it helpful for a mother bird to have dull, plain colors?
answers: No; they are for show and beauty
She is hidden from enemies while sitting on her nest

lessons.title: How Birds Fly
steps: Observation: Watch birds take off, flap, glide and land; wave a fan or a piece of cardboard and feel it push against the air
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "How Birds Fly" (p. 33) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a spread wing showing how the long flight feathers overlap; label what you can and date it
questions: What does a bird press down against when it flaps its wings?
What does a bird's tail do while it flies?
answers: The air
It steers, like a rudder

lessons.title: Eyes and Ears of Birds
steps: Outdoors: Look closely (from a safe distance) at a hen's eye and the side of her head to find her ear opening
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Eyes and Ears of Birds" (p. 36) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a hen's eye with its pupil and colored iris and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: Eyes and Ears of Birds (p. 36)

questions: Does a hen have an extra see-through eyelid?
Where is a hen's ear?
answers: Yes, a thin film lid that slides across the eye
A small opening on the side of the head behind the eye, covered by feathers

lessons.title: The Form and Use of Beaks
steps: Nature walk: Watch a chicken and a duck eat, or birds at a feeder, and notice how each beak picks up its food
Parent previews the background reading on "The Form and Use of Beaks" (p. 37) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw three bird beaks of different shapes and the food each one fits and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: The Form and Use of Beaks (p. 37)

questions: How is a duck's bill different from a hen's beak?
What two parts of a bird are its main tools and weapons?
answers: It is wide, flat and softer at the edges, made for scooping and straining food from water and mud
Its beak and its feet

lessons.title: The Feet of Birds
steps: Go and look: Look for bird tracks in mud or snow; if you can, compare a hen's foot with a duck's foot
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Feet of Birds" (p. 39) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a hen's foot and a webbed duck's foot side by side; add the weather and today's date
questions: What does a hen use her strong toes and claws for?
What does a duck have between its toes that a hen does not?
answers: Scratching the ground to uncover food
Webbing, which helps it swim

lessons.title: Chicken Ways
steps: Observation: Spend time with a hen and her chicks if you can; notice how a chick drinks and listen for the hen's different calls
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Chicken Ways" (p. 41) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a fluffy chick drinking, with its head tipped back; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why does a chick tip its head back when it drinks?
Does a chick chew its food?
answers: It has no way to suck water, so it lets the water run down its throat
No; birds have no teeth, and food is ground up in the gizzard

lessons.title: Pigeons
steps: Outdoors: Watch pigeons in a park or city square; notice how they walk, how they drink and how they coo
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Pigeons" (p. 45) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a pigeon in profile with its head forward mid-step, and add the date and place
questions: How is the way a pigeon drinks different from most birds?
What do pigeon parents feed their newly hatched young?
answers: It sucks up water with its bill down instead of tipping its head back
Pigeon milk, a soft food made in their crop

lessons.title: The Canary and the Goldfinch
steps: Nature walk: Look for goldfinches at thistles, sunflowers or a feeder; if you know someone with a canary, listen to it sing
Parent previews the background reading on "The Canary and the Goldfinch" (p. 49) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a male goldfinch in summer yellow with black cap and wings, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Canary and the Goldfinch (p. 49)

questions: What wild bird is a close relative of the canary?
How does a goldfinch fly?
answers: The goldfinch
In a bouncy, dipping, up-and-down flight

lessons.title: The Robin
steps: Go and look: Keep a robin watch: note the date you see your first robin, then watch one hunting on a lawn
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Robin" (p. 54) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a robin with its brick-red breast, head tipped to look for worms; label what you can and date it
questions: What color is a robin's breast?
When did you see your first robin this spring?
How does a robin hunt worms on the lawn?
answers: Reddish orange (brick red)
It runs, stops, tips its head to look and listen, then pulls the worm out

lessons.title: The Bluebird
steps: Observation: Look for bluebirds in open fields, orchards and along fences; check any nest boxes you can find
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Bluebird" (p. 60) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a bluebird showing its blue back and rusty breast; label what you can and date it
questions: What common bird is the bluebird related to?
Where do bluebirds like to nest?
answers: The robin (both are thrushes)
In holes in trees, posts or nest boxes

units.title: Unit 2: Bird Study II — Nuthatch to Mockingbird

lessons.title: The White-breasted Nuthatch
steps: Outdoors: Watch a tree trunk near a feeder for a nuthatch walking head-first down the bark
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The White-breasted Nuthatch" (p. 63) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a nuthatch upside down on a trunk and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does a nuthatch's way of climbing a tree differ from a woodpecker's?
Does a nuthatch have a black bib like a chickadee?
answers: It can go down the trunk head first; a woodpecker backs down
No

lessons.title: The Chickadee
steps: Nature walk: On a winter day, watch chickadees at a feeder or in the bushes and listen for their call
Parent previews the background reading on "The Chickadee" (p. 66) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a chickadee with its black cap and black bib and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What does the chickadee's call sound like?
Does the chickadee fly south for the winter?
answers: Its own name: chick-a-dee-dee-dee
No, it stays in the North all winter

lessons.title: The Downy Woodpecker
steps: Go and look: Look and listen for a small black-and-white woodpecker tapping on trunks, especially in winter
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Downy Woodpecker" (p. 69) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a downy woodpecker propped on its stiff tail; add the weather and today's date
questions: Which downy woodpeckers have the red patch on the head?
How does the downy use its tail when climbing?
How does the downy help our trees?
answers: Only the males
Its stiff tail feathers prop it against the trunk
It digs out insects and insect eggs hiding in the bark

lessons.title: The Sapsucker
steps: Observation: Search tree trunks (apple, birch, maple) for neat rows of small holes drilled by sapsuckers
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Sapsucker" (p. 73) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a tree trunk with rows of sapsucker holes; add the weather and today's date
questions: What does a sapsucker eat from the holes it drills?
How is the sapsucker different from our other woodpeckers?
answers: Sap, and the insects that come to the sap
It is the one that harms trees by drilling rows of sap holes

lessons.title: The Redheaded Woodpecker
steps: Outdoors: Look along woodland edges, fence posts and dead trees for a bird with an all-red head
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Redheaded Woodpecker" (p. 75) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a red-headed woodpecker showing its red head and white wing patches, and add the date and place
questions: What does the red-headed woodpecker eat besides insects?
Is its whole head red or just a patch?
answers: Nuts, fruit and seeds
The whole head and neck are red

lessons.title: The Flicker or Yellow-hammer
steps: Nature walk: Watch lawns and meadows for a large brown woodpecker feeding on the ground; look for its white rump as it flies
Parent previews the background reading on "The Flicker or Yellow-hammer" (p. 77) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a flicker showing its spotted breast and black crescent, and add the date and place
questions: What insect does the flicker often hunt on the ground?
What does the white patch above its tail do?
answers: Ants
It flashes when the bird flies, helping other flickers follow it

lessons.title: The Meadowlark
steps: Go and look: Walk by a meadow or pasture and listen for the meadowlark's whistled song from a fence post
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Meadowlark" (p. 80) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a meadowlark with its yellow breast and black V; label what you can and date it
questions: What is the black mark on a meadowlark's yellow breast shaped like?
Where does the meadowlark build its nest?
answers: A V (crescent)
On the ground, hidden in the grass

lessons.title: The English Sparrow
steps: Observation: Find house (English) sparrows near buildings and watch how they act around other birds
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The English Sparrow" (p. 84) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a male house sparrow with his black bib; label what you can and date it
questions: Where did the English sparrow come from?
What kind of food is the sparrow's thick, cone-shaped beak made for?
answers: It was brought over from Europe (England)
Seeds
lessons.notes: Comstock's 1911 view of the English (house) sparrow is harsh; today we call it the house sparrow and simply note it is not native.

lessons.title: The Chipping Sparrow
steps: Outdoors: Look in shrubs and vines near the house for a tiny sparrow with a rusty cap; listen for its dry, trilling chip
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Chipping Sparrow" (p. 88) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a chipping sparrow's small cup nest and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What did chipping sparrows like to line their nests with?
How can you tell a chippy from an English sparrow?
answers: Horsehair
It is smaller and slimmer, with a reddish cap and a clear gray breast

lessons.title: The Song Sparrow
steps: Nature walk: In early spring, listen in brushy places for the song sparrow; try to see the dark spot on its streaked breast
Parent previews the background reading on "The Song Sparrow" (p. 91) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a song sparrow singing from a twig and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What mark in the middle of its breast helps you know a song sparrow?
Which comes first in spring, the song sparrow's song or the robin's?
answers: A dark blotch in the center of the streaks
The song sparrow's, often

lessons.title: The Mockingbird
steps: Go and look: If you live where mockingbirds do, listen for a long song full of borrowed notes, even at night
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Mockingbird" (p. 94) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a mockingbird showing its white wing patches; add the weather and today's date
questions: What makes the mockingbird's singing special?
How many other birds' songs did you hear a mockingbird copy?
answers: It copies the songs of other birds and sounds, and it also sings at night

lessons.title: The Catbird
steps: Observation: Listen in thickets and gardens for a cat-like mewing and find the slate-gray catbird
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Catbird" (p. 98) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a catbird with its black cap and rusty patch under the tail; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why is it called a catbird?
Where do catbirds like to nest?
answers: Its call sounds like a cat mewing
Low in thickets, shrubs and hedges

units.title: Unit 3: Bird Study III — Catbird to Winter Nests

lessons.title: The Belted Kingfisher
steps: Outdoors: Visit a stream or pond and watch for a kingfisher perched over the water or diving
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Belted Kingfisher" (p. 101) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a kingfisher with its big head, crest and dagger beak, and add the date and place
questions: What does the kingfisher eat, and how does it catch it?
Where is the kingfisher's nest?
answers: Fish; it dives headfirst into the water
At the end of a tunnel it digs in a bank

lessons.title: The Screech Owl
steps: Nature walk: At dusk, listen for the screech owl's quavering whinny; by day look for owl pellets under evergreens
Parent previews the background reading on "The Screech Owl" (p. 104) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a screech owl with ear tufts and big forward-facing eyes, and add the date and place
questions: Why can an owl fly so silently?
What are some foods the screech owl eats?
answers: Its soft, fringed feathers muffle the sound
Mice, large insects such as grasshoppers, and other small animals

lessons.title: The Red Shouldered and Red Tailed Hawks
steps: Go and look: Watch the sky on a sunny day for hawks soaring in circles; note where one perches
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Red Shouldered and Red Tailed Hawks" (p. 108) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a hawk soaring with wings and tail spread; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Red Shouldered and Red Tailed Hawks (p. 108)

questions: Do most hawks live mainly by stealing chickens?
Why does a soaring hawk suddenly drop to the ground?
answers: No; most eat mice, insects and other small animals
It has spotted prey below
lessons.notes: In 1911 many hawks were shot as pests; today all hawks and owls are protected by law.

lessons.title: The Swallows and the Chimney Swift
steps: Observation: Watch over a field, barn or pond on a summer evening for swallows and swifts catching insects in the air
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Swallows and the Chimney Swift" (p. 112) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw the outline of a barn swallow's forked tail beside a chimney swift; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Swallows and the Chimney Swift (p. 112)

questions: What do swallows eat, and where do they catch it?
Where does the chimney swift build its nest?
answers: Flying insects, caught in the air
Inside chimneys (once in hollow trees)

lessons.title: The Hummingbird
steps: Outdoors: Sit quietly near red or tubular flowers (bee balm, trumpet vine) and watch for a hummingbird
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Hummingbird" (p. 120) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a hummingbird hovering at a flower and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Why can't we see a hummingbird's wings clearly while it flies?
How does a hummingbird get nectar?
answers: They beat too fast
It hovers and pushes its long beak and tongue into the flower

lessons.title: The Red-winged Blackbird
steps: Nature walk: Walk by a marsh or wet ditch in spring and listen for the red-winged blackbird's 'konk-la-ree'
Parent previews the background reading on "The Red-winged Blackbird" (p. 122) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a male red-wing showing red and yellow shoulder patches and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Where do red-winged blackbirds build their nests?
Which parent do the young red-wings look like?
answers: In marshes, among reeds and cattails
The streaky brown mother

lessons.title: The Baltimore Oriole
steps: Go and look: Look high in elms and shade trees for a hanging, pouch-shaped oriole nest; listen for its rich whistle
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Baltimore Oriole" (p. 125) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch an oriole's hanging nest; add the weather and today's date
questions: Who weaves the oriole's nest?
What shape is the oriole's nest?
answers: The mother bird
A deep hanging pouch or bag

lessons.title: The Crow
steps: Observation: Watch crows in a field or parking lot; notice how they walk, what they eat and how they call to each other
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Crow" (p. 129) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a crow walking, showing its shape and beak; add the weather and today's date
questions: How does a crow fly compared with a soaring hawk?
Why do many people think the crow is our smartest common bird?
answers: With steady rowing wingbeats rather than circling and gliding

lessons.title: The Cardinal Grosbeak
steps: Outdoors: Look for the bright red cardinal at feeders and in thickets; listen for its loud whistle
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Cardinal Grosbeak" (p. 133) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a cardinal showing its crest and heavy beak, and add the date and place
questions: What is the cardinal's thick beak made for?
Is the female cardinal as red as the male?
answers: Cracking seeds
No; she is mostly buff-brown with touches of red

lessons.title: Geese
steps: Nature walk: Visit geese at a farm or park pond and watch how they eat, swim and guard each other
Parent previews the background reading on "Geese" (p. 136) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a goose's long neck and broad bill, and add the date and place
questions: What does a goose mostly eat?
How is a goose's neck different from a duck's?
answers: Grass and other plants
It is longer

lessons.title: The Turkey
steps: Go and look: Visit a farm with turkeys (or watch for wild turkeys) and notice the gobbler's strut
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Turkey" (p. 143) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a gobbler strutting with his tail fanned; label what you can and date it
questions: Where did the turkey first come from?
What does the gobbler do to show off?
answers: America (Mexico)
He puffs up, spreads his tail and struts

lessons.title: The Study of Birds’ Nests in Winter
steps: Observation: In winter, when trees are bare, go on a nest hunt and look for old nests in bushes and trees (leave them in place)
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Study of Birds’ Nests in Winter" (p. 147) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw one nest you found, labeling what it is made of; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Study of Birds’ Nests in Winter (p. 147)

questions: Why is winter the best time to study birds' nests?
What materials did you find woven into the nest?
answers: The birds are gone, so we do not disturb them, and bare trees make nests easy to see
lessons.notes: Leave nests where you find them: collecting nests is illegal for most wild birds today.

units.title: Unit 4: Fish Study

lessons.title: The Goldfish
steps: Outdoors: Watch a goldfish in a bowl or a pet-shop tank for ten minutes; notice which fins move when it swims, turns and stops
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Goldfish" (p. 149) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a goldfish with every fin labeled and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Which part of the fish's body pushes it forward most?
How does a fish breathe under water?
answers: The tail (tail fin)
It takes in water through its mouth and passes it over its gills

lessons.title: The Bullhead
steps: Nature walk: Look at a bullhead (catfish) in an aquarium or at a pond; watch how it feels along the bottom
Parent previews the background reading on "The Bullhead" (p. 154) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a bullhead showing its whisker-like barbels and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What are the bullhead's 'whiskers' called, and what are they for?
Does a bullhead have scales?
answers: Barbels; they help it feel and taste for food in the mud
No; its skin is smooth

lessons.title: The Common Sucker
steps: Go and look: At a still pool or aquarium, watch a sucker feeding along the bottom
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Common Sucker" (p. 158) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the sucker's head showing its mouth underneath; add the weather and today's date
questions: Where is the sucker's mouth, and why?
answers: On the underside of its head, for sucking food from the bottom

lessons.title: The Shiner
steps: Observation: Watch a stream or pond edge for a school of small silvery shiners darting in the shallows
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Shiner" (p. 161) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a shiner showing its colors above, on the sides and below; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why is a fish dark on top and pale underneath?
Do shiners usually swim alone or in groups?
answers: So it is hard to see both from above and from below
In groups (schools)

lessons.title: Brook Trout
steps: Outdoors: Visit a clear cold stream and look for trout resting facing upstream; or see them at a hatchery
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Brook Trout" (p. 164) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a brook trout with its spots, and add the date and place
questions: Which way does a trout face when resting in a stream?
Where does a trout lay its eggs?
answers: Upstream, into the current
In a nest scooped in the gravel of a stream bed
lessons.notes: Fishing now needs a license; simply watching trout is the goal here.

lessons.title: The Stickleback
steps: Nature walk: Look in a weedy, still pond or ditch for the tiny stickleback (a fish with spines on its back)
Parent previews the background reading on "The Stickleback" (p. 168) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a stickleback father at his nest, and add the date and place
questions: Which stickleback parent builds the nest and guards it?
What does the stickleback have on its back?
answers: The father
Sharp spines

lessons.title: The Sunfish
steps: Go and look: At a pond, look in the shallows for sunfish guarding round nests in the sand
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Sunfish" (p. 172) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a sunfish showing its flat, round body; label what you can and date it
questions: Why is it called a 'pumpkin seed'?
Which parent guards the sunfish nest?
answers: Its body is flat and roundish like a pumpkin seed
The father

lessons.title: The Johnny Darter
steps: Observation: In a shallow, fast stream, turn your eyes to the stones on the bottom and watch for the little darter resting and darting
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Johnny Darter" (p. 177) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a johnny darter propped on its fins; label what you can and date it
questions: How does the johnny darter rest on the bottom?
Why is it called a darter?
answers: Propped on its paired fins, almost like feet
It darts suddenly from place to place

units.title: Unit 5: Batrachian (Toad and Frog) and Reptile Study

lessons.title: The Common Toad
steps: Outdoors: Hunt for a toad in the garden in the evening; watch how it hops and catches insects with its tongue
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Common Toad" (p. 181) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a toad with its warty skin and gold-rimmed eyes and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does a toad catch insects?
Does touching a toad give you warts?
Why is a toad a friend to the gardener?
answers: It flicks out its long sticky tongue
No
It eats many insects that hurt garden plants

lessons.title: The Tadpole Aquarium
steps: Nature walk: Collect a few tadpoles with some pond water and plants and set up a tadpole aquarium; check it every few days
Parent previews the background reading on "The Tadpole Aquarium" (p. 185) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a tadpole at the stage you see today and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Which legs appear first on a tadpole?
What happens to the tail when the legs are grown?
answers: The hind legs
It is absorbed into the body and disappears

lessons.title: The Tree-frog or Tree-toad
steps: Go and look: On a spring evening, go near a pond and listen to the spring peepers; try to find one with a flashlight
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Tree-frog or Tree-toad" (p. 190) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a tree frog showing its sticky toe pads; add the weather and today's date
questions: What helps a tree frog cling to trees and leaves?
When do you hear the peepers sing?
answers: Sticky pads on the tips of its toes
In early spring, especially in the evening

lessons.title: The Frog
steps: Observation: At a pond edge, watch frogs jump and swim; look for frog eggs in jelly masses
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Frog" (p. 193) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a frog in a jump, showing its long hind legs; add the weather and today's date
questions: How is a frog's skin different from a toad's?
Where does a frog lay its eggs?
answers: It is smooth and slippery, not dry and warty
In masses of jelly in the water

lessons.title: The Newt, Eft or Salamander
steps: Outdoors: After a rain, look on damp woodland paths and under logs for a red eft (put logs back as you found them)
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Newt, Eft or Salamander" (p. 197) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch an eft or salamander with its tail and four legs, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Newt, Eft or Salamander (p. 197)

questions: Why do we find efts mostly after a rain?
How many times does a newt change its form?
answers: They need damp places and come out when the ground is wet
Three: water larva, land eft, then water newt again

lessons.title: The Garter or Garden Snake
steps: Nature walk: Look for a garter snake sunning on a rock or path edge on a warm day; watch it flick its tongue
Parent previews the background reading on "The Garter or Garden Snake" (p. 201) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a garter snake with its stripes, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Garter or Garden Snake (p. 201)

questions: Why does a snake flick its tongue in and out?
Is the garter snake dangerous to people?
answers: To pick up smells from the air
No, it is harmless
lessons.notes: Watch snakes without handling them unless an adult knows the species is harmless.

lessons.title: The Milk Snake, or Spotted Adder
steps: Go and look: Ask at a barn or farm about milk snakes; look (do not touch) for a snake with reddish-brown blotches
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Milk Snake, or Spotted Adder" (p. 204) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw the milk snake's blotched pattern; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Milk Snake, or Spotted Adder (p. 204)

questions: Does the milk snake really drink milk from cows?
How does the milk snake kill its prey?
answers: No; it comes to barns to hunt mice and rats
It squeezes it (constriction)
lessons.notes: Look, don't touch: let an adult confirm any snake before getting close.

lessons.title: The Water Snake
steps: Observation: Walk along a stream or pond on a sunny day and look for a snake basking on rocks or branches over the water (watch only)
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Water Snake" (p. 206) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a water snake on a sunny branch over water; label what you can and date it
questions: Why does the water snake live near water?
answers: Its food, such as fish and frogs, lives there
lessons.notes: Northern water snakes are not venomous but do bite; in the South, keep clear of any water snake (cottonmouths look similar).

lessons.title: The Turtle
steps: Outdoors: Look for turtles sunning on logs at a pond; watch how they slide into the water when startled
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Turtle" (p. 208) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a turtle's top shell showing its plates and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What is the turtle's shell for?
What does a turtle do when frightened?
answers: Protection from enemies
Pulls its head, legs and tail into its shell or slides into the water

units.title: Unit 6: Mammal Study I — Wild Neighbors

lessons.title: The Cotton-tail Rabbit
steps: Nature walk: Look for rabbit tracks in snow or soft dirt and watch for cottontails at dusk on a lawn edge
Parent previews the background reading on "The Cotton-tail Rabbit" (p. 213) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw rabbit tracks, showing where the big hind feet land and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Why are a rabbit's long ears useful?
What does a cottontail eat in winter?
answers: They help it hear danger coming
Bark, twigs and buds

lessons.title: The Muskrat
steps: Go and look: At a marsh or slow stream, look for muskrat houses of cattails and watch for a swimmer with a thin tail
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Muskrat" (p. 218) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a muskrat swimming with its tail; add the weather and today's date
questions: What is a muskrat's house made of?
How is the muskrat's tail shaped, and what is it for?
answers: Cattails, reeds and mud
Flattened side to side; it helps steer and push in the water

lessons.title: The House Mouse
steps: Observation: Look for signs of mice in a shed, barn or attic: droppings, chewed paper or seed husks
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The House Mouse" (p. 224) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a mouse with its big ears, whiskers and long tail; add the weather and today's date
questions: What do mice use to build their nests?
Why are mice hard to catch?
answers: Soft shredded materials like paper, cloth and grass
They are small, quick, quiet, and their color blends in

lessons.title: The Woodchuck
steps: Outdoors: Look in fields and along fences for woodchuck burrows and watch for one sitting up to look around
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Woodchuck" (p. 229) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a woodchuck sitting up at its burrow, and add the date and place
questions: What does the woodchuck do all winter?
What does a woodchuck eat?
answers: It hibernates (sleeps deeply) in its burrow
Green plants like clover and grass

lessons.title: The Red Squirrel or Chickaree
steps: Nature walk: In woods or a park, watch a red squirrel; look for piles of cone scales where it has eaten, and tracks in snow
Parent previews the background reading on "The Red Squirrel or Chickaree" (p. 233) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch squirrel tracks in snow, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Red Squirrel or Chickaree (p. 233)

questions: What does a red squirrel often eat in winter?
Where does it store food?
answers: Seeds from pine and spruce cones, and stored nuts
In hidden caches in the ground, hollow trees and under logs

lessons.title: Furry
steps: Go and look: Watch a squirrel for ten minutes and notice everything it does with its tail
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Furry" (p. 238) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a squirrel using its tail; label what you can and date it
questions: What is this chapter about?
answers: Furry, a baby red squirrel that was raised as a pet

lessons.title: The Chipmunk
steps: Observation: Look along stone walls and woodpiles for a chipmunk; watch its cheeks when it gathers food
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Chipmunk" (p. 240) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a chipmunk with its stripes and full cheeks; label what you can and date it
questions: What does the chipmunk carry in its cheek pouches?
Does the chipmunk live more in trees or on the ground?
answers: Seeds and nuts to store
On the ground

lessons.title: The Little Brown Bat
steps: Outdoors: On a summer evening, watch the sky at dusk for bats darting after insects
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Little Brown Bat" (p. 243) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a bat with wings spread showing its finger bones and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What are a bat's wings made of?
How does a bat rest?
answers: Skin stretched between very long finger bones
Hanging upside down by its feet

lessons.title: The Skunk
steps: Nature walk: Look (from far away!) for skunk signs: small cone-shaped holes in a lawn where it dug for grubs
Parent previews the background reading on "The Skunk" (p. 247) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a skunk with its white stripes and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does a skunk protect itself?
How does the skunk help farmers?
answers: With a strong-smelling spray
It eats grubs, mice and harmful insects
lessons.notes: Keep well away from skunks; look only for their signs.

lessons.title: The Raccoon
steps: Go and look: Look in mud along streams for raccoon tracks that look like little hands
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Raccoon" (p. 250) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch raccoon tracks beside a stream; add the weather and today's date
questions: When is the raccoon active?
What makes a raccoon's tracks look like a child's hand?
answers: At night
It has long, finger-like toes
lessons.notes: Never approach a raccoon; wild ones can carry rabies.

units.title: Unit 7: Mammal Study II — Wolf, Fox and Farm Animals

lessons.title: The Wolf
steps: Observation: Look at a dog you know and notice which of its habits might come from wild wolf ancestors (circling before lying down, burying bones)
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Wolf" (p. 255) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a wolf howling; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why does the book study the wolf before the fox and dog?
How do wolves hunt?
answers: Knowing the wolf helps us understand its relatives, the fox and the dog
Together in packs

lessons.title: The Fox
steps: Outdoors: Look for fox tracks in snow along a field edge; notice they go in a nearly straight line
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Fox" (p. 257) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a red fox with its bushy tail, and add the date and place
questions: Where do foxes raise their young?
What color is the tip of a red fox's tail?
answers: In a den, often an underground burrow
White

lessons.title: Dogs
steps: Nature walk: Watch a dog closely: its nose, ears, feet and tail, and how it 'talks' with its body
Parent previews the background reading on "Dogs" (p. 261) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a dog's paw showing its pads and claws, and add the date and place
questions: What wild animals did dogs come from?
Can a dog pull its claws in like a cat?
answers: Wolf-like animals
No

lessons.title: The Cat
steps: Go and look: Watch a cat stalk, pounce and wash itself; look at its eyes in bright light and dim light
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Cat" (p. 268) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a cat's eye with the pupil narrow, then wide; label what you can and date it
questions: What happens to a cat's pupils in bright light?
How does a cat catch its prey?
answers: They become narrow slits
It waits or creeps in hiding, then springs

lessons.title: The Goat
steps: Observation: Visit goats at a farm or petting zoo and watch them climb, eat and call
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Goat" (p. 275) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a goat with its horns and beard; label what you can and date it
questions: What do goats like to climb on?
What can we get from goats?
answers: Rocks and high places
Milk, cheese, meat, hair and leather

lessons.title: The Sheep
steps: Outdoors: Visit sheep and watch how the flock follows a leader and stays together
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Sheep" (p. 281) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a sheep with its woolly coat and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What do we get from a sheep's fleece?
Why does the flock follow a leader?
answers: Wool
Wild sheep escaped danger by following a leader over the mountains

lessons.title: The Horse
steps: Nature walk: Visit a horse and look at its legs, hooves, ears and eyes; watch how its ears show its mood
Parent previews the background reading on "The Horse" (p. 286) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a horse with its parts labeled and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What two qualities helped wild horses escape their enemies?
What does a horse use to defend itself?
answers: Strength and speed
Its hooves (kicking) and teeth

lessons.title: Cattle
steps: Go and look: Watch cows in a pasture: how they graze, lie down and chew their cud
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Cattle" (p. 295) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a cow lying down chewing its cud; add the weather and today's date
questions: What is a cow doing when it chews its cud?
What are cattle raised for today?
answers: Chewing again food it swallowed earlier and brought back up
Milk, meat and leather

lessons.title: The Pig
steps: Observation: Visit pigs at a farm and watch them use their snouts to root; listen to their different noises
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Pig" (p. 303) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a pig's snout; add the weather and today's date
questions: What does a pig use its snout for?
Are pigs naturally dirty animals?
answers: Rooting and digging in the ground for food
No; they are clean when given room, and wallow in mud to keep cool

units.title: Unit 8: Insect Study I — Life Histories, Butterflies and Moths

lessons.title: The Life History of Insects
steps: Outdoors: Go on an insect hunt and find insects at different stages: eggs, caterpillars or grubs, cocoons and adults
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Life History of Insects" (p. 308) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch the four stages of an insect's life (egg, larva, pupa, adult), and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Life History of Insects (p. 308)

questions: What are the four stages of complete metamorphosis?
What is a caterpillar the larva of?
answers: Egg, larva, pupa, adult
A butterfly or moth
lessons.notes: Comstock describes killing insects for collections; today a jar, a lens and a photo are enough.

lessons.title: The Structure of Insects
steps: Nature walk: Catch a grasshopper or beetle in a jar and count its body parts and legs, then let it go
Parent previews the background reading on "The Structure of Insects" (p. 312) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch an insect with head, thorax and abdomen labeled, and add the date and place
questions: How many legs does an insect have?
What are an insect's three body parts called?
answers: Six
Head, thorax and abdomen

lessons.title: The Black Swallow-tail Butterfly
steps: Go and look: Look on parsley, carrot or dill plants for the green-and-black striped caterpillar of the black swallowtail
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Black Swallow-tail Butterfly" (p. 315) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw the swallowtail caterpillar on a carrot-family leaf; label what you can and date it
questions: What does the swallowtail caterpillar do when it is disturbed?
On what plants does it feed?
answers: Pushes out orange scent horns behind its head
Carrot-family plants like parsley, carrot and dill

lessons.title: The Monarch Butterfly
steps: Observation: Search milkweed plants for monarch eggs, caterpillars and green chrysalises
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Monarch Butterfly" (p. 320) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a monarch caterpillar or chrysalis on milkweed; label what you can and date it
questions: What plant do monarch caterpillars eat?
Why do birds leave monarchs alone?
What does the monarch do in the fall?
answers: Milkweed
They taste bad
Migrates south

lessons.title: The Isabella Tiger Moth or Woolly Bear
steps: Outdoors: In fall, look for woolly bear caterpillars crossing roads and paths; count its legs
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Isabella Tiger Moth or Woolly Bear" (p. 326) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a woolly bear with its black and rusty bands and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: The Isabella Tiger Moth or Woolly Bear (p. 326)

questions: Where is the woolly bear hurrying to in the fall?
What does the woolly bear become?
answers: A sheltered place to spend the winter
The Isabella tiger moth

lessons.title: The Cecropia
steps: Nature walk: In winter, search shrubs and fruit trees for large silk cocoons fastened along twigs
Parent previews the background reading on "The Cecropia" (p. 330) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a cecropia cocoon on a twig and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: In what form does the cecropia spend the winter?
What did the caterpillar make the cocoon from?
answers: As a pupa inside a silk cocoon
Silk

lessons.title: The Promethea
steps: Go and look: Look on wild cherry, lilac or spicebush in winter for a dry leaf hanging oddly from a twig; it may hide a cocoon
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Promethea" (p. 336) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a promethea cocoon wrapped in a leaf; add the weather and today's date
questions: How does the promethea keep its cocoon on the tree all winter?
answers: It ties the leaf stem to the twig with silk

lessons.title: The Hummingbird, or Sphinx, Moths
steps: Observation: At dusk, watch flowers like petunias or honeysuckle for a large moth hovering like a hummingbird; check tomato plants for hornworms
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Hummingbird, or Sphinx, Moths" (p. 340) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a sphinx caterpillar showing its 'horn'; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: The Hummingbird, or Sphinx, Moths (p. 340)

questions: What does a sphinx caterpillar have on its last segment?
Why are these called hummingbird moths?
answers: A horn or an eye-spot
They hover at flowers like hummingbirds

lessons.title: The Codling Moth
steps: Outdoors: Cut open a wormy apple and look for the tunnel and the caterpillar
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Codling Moth" (p. 347) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a cut apple showing the tunnel to the core, and add the date and place
questions: Where does the codling moth lay its egg?
What part of the apple does the larva head for?
answers: On or near the apple
The core

units.title: Unit 9: Insect Study II — Leaf-dwellers, Grasshoppers and Crickets

lessons.title: Leaf-miners
steps: Nature walk: Look closely at leaves (columbine, oak, apple) for wiggly pale trails and blister-like blotches
Parent previews the background reading on "Leaf-miners" (p. 352) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a leaf with a mine trail, and add the date and place
questions: What makes the winding lines inside a leaf?
Does the trail get wider or narrower as it goes on? Why?
answers: A tiny larva eating its way between the top and bottom of the leaf
Wider, because the larva grows as it eats

lessons.title: The Leaf-rollers
steps: Go and look: Look for rolled-up or tied-together leaves on trees and shrubs; gently open one to see who lives inside
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Leaf-rollers" (p. 357) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a rolled leaf and the silk that holds it; label what you can and date it
questions: What holds a leaf-roller's leaf in a roll?
Why does the insect live inside a rolled leaf?
answers: Silk threads
It gets shelter and food at once, hidden from enemies

lessons.title: The Gall-dwellers
steps: Observation: Look for galls (round swellings) on oak leaves, goldenrod stems or willow tips
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Gall-dwellers" (p. 360) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a gall, and a cut-open one showing the cell inside; label what you can and date it
questions: Who lives inside a gall?
What does the gall do for the insect inside?
answers: A young insect (larva)
It gives it food and a protective home

lessons.title: The Grasshopper
steps: Outdoors: In a grassy field, catch a grasshopper gently and watch how it jumps, eats and cleans itself
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Grasshopper" (p. 365) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a grasshopper with its long jumping legs and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Which legs does a grasshopper use for jumping?
How does its color protect it?
answers: The big hind legs
It blends with the grass and soil

lessons.title: The Katydid
steps: Nature walk: On a late-summer evening, listen in the treetops for the katydid's rasping 'katy-did, katy-didn't'
Parent previews the background reading on "The Katydid" (p. 370) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a katydid with its leaf-like green wings and long antennae and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does the male katydid make its song?
Where do katydids live?
answers: By rubbing its wing covers together
In trees

lessons.title: The Black Cricket
steps: Go and look: Turn over boards and stones in a field to find black crickets; listen for cricket chirps at night
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Black Cricket" (p. 373) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a cricket, showing the mother's long egg-laying tube; add the weather and today's date
questions: Which crickets sing, males or females?
What is the long tube at the tip of the mother cricket's body for?
answers: The males
Laying her eggs in the ground (it is called the ovipositor)

lessons.title: The Snowy Tree-cricket
steps: Observation: On a warm August night, listen for the steady, even trill of snowy tree crickets in shrubs; count the chirps for 15 seconds
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Snowy Tree-cricket" (p. 377) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a pale green snowy tree cricket; add the weather and today's date
questions: How can a snowy tree cricket tell you the temperature?
What color is the snowy tree cricket?
answers: It chirps faster when it is warmer, so counting chirps gives an estimate
Pale green, almost white

lessons.title: The Cockroach
steps: Outdoors: If you can, watch a cockroach in a jar or insect exhibit (never handle wild ones); note its flat body and long legs
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Cockroach" (p. 378) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a cockroach's flat body from above, and add the date and place
questions: Why is the cockroach's body so flat?
Are its legs made for running fast?
answers: So it can squeeze into narrow cracks
Yes

lessons.title: How to Make an Aquarium for Insects
steps: Nature walk: Make a simple insect aquarium: a large glass jar with sand, a few stones, pond plants and pond water
Parent previews the background reading on "How to Make an Aquarium for Insects" (p. 380) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch your aquarium and what you put in it, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: How to Make an Aquarium for Insects (p. 380)

questions: Why should an aquarium have living water plants in it?
Why is glass the best container?
answers: They give oxygen to the water
You can see everything inside it

units.title: Unit 10: Insect Study III — Water Insects, Flies and Beetles

lessons.title: The Dragon-flies and Damsel-flies
steps: Go and look: Watch a pond on a sunny day for dragonflies and damselflies; notice how each one holds its wings when resting
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Dragon-flies and Damsel-flies" (p. 382) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a dragonfly and a damselfly at rest, showing their wings; label what you can and date it
questions: How can you tell a damselfly from a dragonfly when they rest?
Where do young dragonflies (nymphs) live?
answers: A damselfly folds its wings over its back; a dragonfly holds them out flat
In the water

lessons.title: The Caddis-worms and the Caddis-flies
steps: Observation: Look on the bottom of a clear stream for little cases made of sticks, sand or pebbles that crawl
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Caddis-worms and the Caddis-flies" (p. 387) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a caddis-worm case and what it is made of; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Caddis-worms and the Caddis-flies (p. 387)

questions: What does a caddis-worm build its house from?
What does the caddis-worm become as an adult?
answers: Bits of sticks, leaves, sand or tiny stones held with silk
A caddis-fly

lessons.title: The Aphids or Plant Lice
steps: Outdoors: Look on rose shoots, milkweed or garden plants for clusters of tiny aphids; watch whether ants visit them
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Aphids or Plant Lice" (p. 392) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw an aphid with its sucking beak and the two tubes on its back and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: The Aphids or Plant Lice (p. 392)

questions: How does an aphid feed?
Name an enemy of the aphids
answers: It sucks plant juices through a beak-like tube
Ladybirds (and their larvae), lacewing larvae, and other insects

lessons.title: The Ant-lion
steps: Nature walk: Search dry, sandy spots under porches or overhangs for small cone-shaped pits; gently drop in an ant and watch
Parent previews the background reading on "The Ant-lion" (p. 395) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw an ant-lion pit in cross section and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does the ant-lion catch its food?
What is another name for the ant-lion?
answers: It waits at the bottom of a sandy pit and grabs ants that slide in
Doodle-bug

lessons.title: Mother Lace-wing and the Aphis-lion
steps: Go and look: Look on leaves near aphid colonies for lace-wing eggs, each perched on top of a thin silk stalk
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Mother Lace-wing and the Aphis-lion" (p. 397) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a lace-wing's egg on its stalk and the green adult; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: Mother Lace-wing and the Aphis-lion (p. 397)

questions: Why does the lace-wing lay her eggs on tall stalks?
What does the aphis-lion eat?
answers: So the first larva to hatch cannot eat the other eggs
Aphids (plant lice)

lessons.title: The Mosquito
steps: Observation: Look in a rain barrel, bucket or puddle for mosquito 'wrigglers'; watch them rise to the surface to breathe
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Mosquito" (p. 400) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a wriggler hanging from the water's surface; add the weather and today's date
questions: How does a mosquito wriggler breathe?
Why should we empty standing water around the house?
answers: Through a tube at its tail end that it pokes up to the surface
So mosquitoes cannot breed in it
lessons.notes: Empty any standing water you used once you've watched the wrigglers.

lessons.title: The House-fly
steps: Outdoors: Watch a fly (through a window) clean its legs and head; with a lens look at its eyes
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The House-fly" (p. 405) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a fly cleaning its front legs, and add the date and place
questions: How does a fly carry germs to our food?
How many wings does a house-fly have?
answers: It walks on filth and then on food, carrying germs on its feet and body
Two

lessons.title: The Colorado Potato-beetle
steps: Nature walk: Look on potato plants (or eggplant) for striped potato beetles and their orange eggs
Parent previews the background reading on "The Colorado Potato-beetle" (p. 409) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a striped Colorado potato beetle, and add the date and place
questions: What plants does the Colorado potato-beetle eat?
What protects a beetle's flying wings?
answers: Potatoes and their relatives
Hard wing covers

lessons.title: The Ladybird
steps: Go and look: Search plants with aphids for ladybirds and their spiky, alligator-like larvae
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Ladybird" (p. 413) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a ladybird and its larva; label what you can and date it
questions: What do ladybirds and their larvae eat?
Does a young ladybird look like its parent?
answers: Aphids (plant lice)
No; it is a long, spiky larva

lessons.title: The Firefly
steps: Observation: On a warm summer night, watch fireflies flash over a lawn or meadow; count the seconds between flashes
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Firefly" (p. 416) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a firefly showing its glowing tail segments; label what you can and date it
questions: What kind of insect is a firefly?
Is a firefly's light hot?
answers: A beetle
No, it is a cold light

units.title: Unit 11: Insect Study IV — Ants, Wasps and Bees

lessons.title: The Ways of the Ant
steps: Outdoors: Follow a line of ants from food to their nest; lift a flat stone to see an ant nest (put it back gently)
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Ways of the Ant" (p. 419) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw an ant trail from food to nest and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: The Ways of the Ant (p. 419)

questions: What are the stages of an ant's life?
Do ants on a trail follow the same path?
answers: Egg, larva, pupa, adult
Yes, mostly; they follow scent trails

lessons.title: How to Make a Lubbock Ant-Nest
steps: Nature walk: With a parent, build a simple observation ant nest between two panes of glass (or a jar of soil) and add ants from one colony
Parent previews the background reading on "How to Make a Lubbock Ant-Nest" (p. 423) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw your ant nest design and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: How to Make a Lubbock Ant-Nest (p. 423)

questions: Why should the glass of the ant nest be covered most of the time?
Why should all your ants come from the same nest?
answers: Ants like darkness in their nest
Ants from different nests fight each other

lessons.title: The Ant-Nest and What May be Seen Within it
steps: Go and look: Watch your ant nest (or an outdoor nest) and see how ants carry food and young
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Ant-Nest and What May be Seen Within it" (p. 425) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch an ant carrying a pupa in its jaws; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: The Ant-Nest and What May be Seen Within it (p. 425)

questions: How do ants carry their young?
How do ants share food with each other?
answers: In their jaws
They pass food mouth to mouth

lessons.title: The Mud-dauber
steps: Observation: Look under eaves, porches and bridges for the mud tubes of mud-dauber wasps (look but don't touch)
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Mud-dauber" (p. 429) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a mud-dauber's mud nest tubes; add the weather and today's date
questions: What does the mud-dauber build its nest from?
What does the mother wasp put in each cell for her young?
answers: Mud
Paralyzed spiders for food
lessons.notes: Mud-daubers rarely sting, but still look without touching.

lessons.title: The Yellow-jacket
steps: Outdoors: From a safe distance, look for paper wasp nests hanging under eaves or in bushes; find an old empty one in winter
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Yellow-jacket" (p. 432) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch an empty paper nest showing the combs inside, and add the date and place
questions: What do wasps make their paper from?
What happens to most of a yellow-jacket colony in winter?
answers: Wood they chew into pulp
They die; only young queens survive the winter
lessons.notes: Never disturb an active wasp nest; study an empty one found in winter.

lessons.title: The Leaf-cutter Bee
steps: Nature walk: Look at rose or lilac leaves for neat round and oval holes cut from the edges
Parent previews the background reading on "The Leaf-cutter Bee" (p. 436) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a leaf with leaf-cutter bee cuts, and add the date and place
questions: What does the leaf-cutter bee do with the leaf pieces?
Which shape of cut piece is used for the lids?
answers: Rolls them into cells for its nest
Round ones

lessons.title: The Little Carpenter Bee
steps: Go and look: Look at broken or cut stems of sumac, elder or raspberry for a small hole with a tunnel going down the pith
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Little Carpenter Bee" (p. 439) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a stem split open showing the bee's cells; label what you can and date it
questions: Where does the little carpenter bee make her nest?
Does the little carpenter bee live in a big colony?
answers: In a tunnel she digs in the pith of a stem
No; she lives alone

lessons.title: The Bumblebee
steps: Observation: Watch bumblebees visiting clover and other flowers; notice the pollen baskets on their hind legs
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Bumblebee" (p. 442) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a bumblebee with full pollen baskets; label what you can and date it
questions: How do bumblebees help farm crops and wildflowers?
Will a bumblebee sting?
answers: They carry pollen from flower to flower
Females can if handled or bothered

lessons.title: The Honey-bee
steps: Outdoors: Watch honey bees at flowers; if possible visit a beekeeper. Notice the pollen loads on their legs
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Honey-bee" (p. 445) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a honey bee with its parts labeled and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What three kinds of bees live in a hive?
What do worker bees do?
answers: Queen, drones and workers
Gather food, make wax and comb, care for young, and guard and clean the hive
lessons.notes: Keep calm and still around bees; anyone with a bee allergy should watch from a distance.

lessons.title: The Honey-comb
steps: Nature walk: Look at a piece of honeycomb (from a store or a beekeeper) and count the sides of a cell
Parent previews the background reading on "The Honey-comb" (p. 451) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a few honeycomb cells and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How many sides does a honeycomb cell have?
Why is the six-sided shape a good choice?
answers: Six
It fits together without gaps and saves wax and space

lessons.title: Industries of the Hive and the Observation Hive
steps: Go and look: Visit an observation hive at a nature center or watch a video of the inside of a hive
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Industries of the Hive and the Observation Hive" (p. 453) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the layout of a hive with brood and honey areas; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: Industries of the Hive and the Observation Hive (p. 453)

questions: What do bees make wax from?
What is bee-bread?
answers: It comes from glands on the worker's body (made from honey she eats)
Stored pollen used to feed young bees

units.title: Unit 12: Other Invertebrates — Snail, Earthworm, Crayfish and Spiders

lessons.title: The Garden Snail
steps: Observation: After a rain, look for snails on walls, plants and paths; let one crawl on a piece of glass and watch from underneath
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Garden Snail" (p. 458) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a snail with its shell, foot and feelers; add the weather and today's date
questions: What does a snail leave behind it as it crawls?
Where are a snail's eyes?
answers: A trail of slime (mucus)
At the tips of its long upper feelers

lessons.title: The Earthworm
steps: Outdoors: After a rain, find earthworms on a path or dig carefully in a garden; watch how one moves
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Earthworm" (p. 462) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch an earthworm, showing its segments and the band, and add the date and place
questions: How do earthworms help the soil?
Does an earthworm have eyes?
answers: They loosen it, let in air and water, and mix in leaves
No, but it can sense light

lessons.title: The Crayfish
steps: Nature walk: Turn over stones in a shallow stream to find crayfish; watch them swim backward
Parent previews the background reading on "The Crayfish" (p. 466) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a crayfish from above with its pincers, and add the date and place
questions: How does a crayfish escape quickly?
Can a crayfish grow back a lost leg?
answers: By flipping its tail to dart backward
Yes
lessons.notes: Crayfish pinch: lift by the back of the shell or just watch.

lessons.title: Daddy Longlegs, or Grandfather Greybeard
steps: Go and look: Look on walls, fences and grass for a daddy longlegs; count its legs
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Daddy Longlegs, or Grandfather Greybeard" (p. 472) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a daddy longlegs with all its legs; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: Daddy Longlegs, or Grandfather Greybeard (p. 472)

questions: How many legs does a daddy longlegs have?
Is a daddy longlegs an insect?
answers: Eight
No; insects have six legs. It is related to spiders

lessons.title: Spiders
steps: Observation: Search corners of a shed or porch for cobwebs and find where the spider hides
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Spiders" (p. 475) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a cobweb and the spider's hiding spot; label what you can and date it
questions: How many legs does a spider have?
Where does the spider make its silk?
answers: Eight
In spinnerets at the tip of its abdomen

lessons.title: The Funnel-web
steps: Outdoors: On a dewy morning, look in the grass for funnel-shaped webs; touch one lightly with a grass stem
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Funnel-web" (p. 477) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a funnel web with its back door and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Where does the grass spider wait?
Why does the web have a back door?
answers: In the narrow tube of the funnel
So the spider can escape if danger comes

lessons.title: The Orb-web
steps: Nature walk: Find an orb web in the garden on a dewy morning; trace the spokes and the spiral
Parent previews the background reading on "The Orb-web" (p. 478) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw an orb web showing spokes and spiral and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Which threads in an orb web are sticky?
How does the spider know when something is caught?
answers: The spiral threads
It feels the web shake

lessons.title: The Filmy Dome
steps: Go and look: On a sunny morning, look in bushes and evergreens for tiny dome-shaped webs
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Filmy Dome" (p. 483) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the filmy dome web with the spider underneath; add the weather and today's date
questions: Where does the dome spider hang?
What are the threads above the dome for?
answers: Under the top of the dome, back down
Tripping flying insects so they fall onto the dome

lessons.title: Ballooning Spiders
steps: Observation: On a warm fall day, look for silk threads floating through the air or tiny spiders on fence posts letting out silk
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Ballooning Spiders" (p. 484) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a young spider ballooning on its thread; add the weather and today's date
questions: How do young spiders travel far from home?
Why is it good for young spiders to spread out?
answers: They float through the air on silk threads (ballooning)
So they don't crowd each other and run out of food

lessons.title: The White Crab-Spider
steps: Outdoors: Look closely inside white and yellow flowers for a crab spider waiting to catch visitors
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The White Crab-Spider" (p. 485) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a crab spider on a flower, and add the date and place
questions: Why is it called a crab spider?
How does it hide from insects?
answers: It holds its legs out and walks sideways like a crab
Its color matches the flower

lessons.title: How the Spider Mothers Take Care of their Young
steps: Nature walk: Look for spider egg sacs on fences, under bark, or carried by wolf spiders
Parent previews the background reading on "How the Spider Mothers Take Care of their Young" (p. 487) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a spider egg sac, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: How the Spider Mothers Take Care of their Young (p. 487)

questions: What do spider mothers wrap their eggs in?
How does a wolf spider mother carry her eggs?
answers: Silk sacs
Attached to her spinnerets

units.title: Unit 13: Beginning Plant Study and Spring Wild Flowers

lessons.title: Beginning Plant Study: Growing Plants and Making Them Comfortable
steps: Go and look: Plant a few bean, pea or flower seeds in a pot or window box and care for them; take a walk to enjoy flowers
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Beginning Plant Study: Growing Plants and Making Them Comfortable" (p. 489) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw what you planted and where; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: How to Begin the Study of Plants and Flowers (p. 489)
Read: How to Make Plants Comfortable (p. 490)

questions: What is the best way for young children to begin plant study?
What does a plant need to be comfortable?
answers: By growing plants and learning to love flowers
Good soil, water, light and air

lessons.title: The Parts of a Flower, Its Use, and Its Insect Partners
steps: Observation: Pick a large, simple flower (lily, tulip, or wild rose) and find each part
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Parts of a Flower, Its Use, and Its Insect Partners" (p. 492) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a flower with petals, sepals, stamens and pistil labeled; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: How to Teach the Names of the Parts of a Flower (p. 492)
Read: Teach the Use of a Flower (p. 493)

questions: What is the main job of a flower?
What do bees carry from flower to flower?
answers: To make seeds
Pollen

lessons.title: Where Plants Grow, and Seed Germination
steps: Outdoors: Soak bean seeds overnight and plant some in a clear jar against wet paper to watch them sprout; note where plants grow on your walks
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Where Plants Grow, and Seed Germination" (p. 495) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a sprouting bean, day by day and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: The Relation of Plants to Geography (p. 495)

questions: What comes out of a seed first, the root or the shoot?
Why do some plants grow only in woods and others only in fields?
answers: The root
Each needs a certain amount of light, water and type of soil

lessons.title: The Hepatica
steps: Nature walk: In very early spring, look in moist woods for hepatica flowers among last year's leaves
Parent previews the background reading on "The Hepatica" (p. 496) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a hepatica plant with its three-lobed leaves and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: When are hepatica flower buds made?
What shape are hepatica leaves?
answers: The fall before they bloom
Three-lobed (like a liver)

lessons.title: The Yellow Adder’s Tongue
steps: Go and look: In spring woods, look for patches of mottled leaves and nodding yellow lily-like flowers (trout lily)
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Yellow Adder’s Tongue" (p. 499) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the mottled leaf and nodding flower; add the weather and today's date
questions: What family does the adder's tongue belong to?
What does each plant grow from deep underground?
answers: The lily family
A corm

lessons.title: Bloodroot
steps: Observation: In early spring woods, find bloodroot; notice how the leaf wraps around the flower bud
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Bloodroot" (p. 503) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a bloodroot leaf wrapped around its bud; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why is it called bloodroot?
Where does the plant store food for its early flower?
answers: Its root has red-orange juice
In its thick underground rootstock

lessons.title: The Trillium
steps: Outdoors: In spring woods, find a trillium and count its leaves, sepals and petals (don't pick it)
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Trillium" (p. 506) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a trillium seen from above, and add the date and place
questions: Why is it called a trillium?
Why should we not pick trilliums?
answers: Its parts come in threes: three leaves, three sepals, three petals
Picking the leaves with the flower can kill the plant

lessons.title: Dutchman’s Breeches and Squirrel Corn
steps: Nature walk: In rich spring woods, look for Dutchman's breeches with its upside-down, pants-shaped flowers
Parent previews the background reading on "Dutchman’s Breeches and Squirrel Corn" (p. 509) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a Dutchman's breeches flower, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: Dutchman’s Breeches and Squirrel Corn (p. 509)

questions: What does the Dutchman's breeches flower look like?
What insect can reach its nectar best?
answers: A tiny pair of white pants hanging upside down
Bumblebees (long-tongued bees)

lessons.title: Jack-in-the-Pulpit
steps: Go and look: In damp woods, look for Jack-in-the-pulpit; gently lift the hood to peek at 'Jack'
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Jack-in-the-Pulpit" (p. 512) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw Jack-in-the-pulpit with its hood and the 'Jack' inside; label what you can and date it
questions: Where are Jack-in-the-pulpit's real flowers?
What does the plant have in the fall?
answers: Tiny flowers at the base of 'Jack,' hidden inside the striped hood
A cluster of bright red berries

lessons.title: The Violet
steps: Observation: Find violets in a lawn or woods; look inside one for the lines pointing to the nectar
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Violet" (p. 515) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a violet flower front view with its guide lines; label what you can and date it
questions: What do the lines on a violet's petals do?
Where is the violet's nectar kept?
answers: Guide insects to the nectar
In a spur at the back of the lower petal

lessons.title: The May Apple or Mandrake
steps: Outdoors: In spring woods, look for a colony of May apples with their umbrella leaves; peek under for the flower
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The May Apple or Mandrake" (p. 519) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a May apple with its umbrella leaves and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: The May Apple or Mandrake (p. 519)

questions: Why do May apples grow in big patches?
Which part of the May apple is poisonous?
answers: They spread by underground stems
The leaves, roots and unripe fruit (only the ripe fruit is edible)
lessons.notes: May apple leaves, roots and unripe fruit are poisonous; wash hands after handling.

units.title: Unit 14: Wild Flowers II — Bluets to Cat-tail

lessons.title: The Bluets
steps: Nature walk: In spring meadows, look for little pale-blue bluets with yellow centers; compare a few flowers closely with a lens
Parent previews the background reading on "The Bluets" (p. 523) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a bluet flower with its four petals and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How many petals does a bluet have?
