Why do bluets have two forms of flowers?
answers: Four
To make sure pollen goes from one plant to another (cross-pollination)

lessons.title: The Yellow Lady’s Slipper, or Moccasin Flower
steps: Go and look: If you live near rich woods, look for a lady's slipper orchid in late spring (look but never pick)
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Yellow Lady’s Slipper, or Moccasin Flower" (p. 525) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the lady's slipper's pouch; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: The Yellow Lady’s Slipper, or Moccasin Flower (p. 525)

questions: What family does the lady's slipper belong to?
How do insects carry its pollen?
answers: The orchids
They crawl into the pouch and must squeeze out past the pollen to escape

lessons.title: The Common Buttercup
steps: Observation: In a sunny meadow, pick a buttercup and look at its shiny petals; count petals and stamens
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Common Buttercup" (p. 528) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a buttercup flower; add the weather and today's date
questions: How is a buttercup different from a daisy?
How many petals does a common buttercup usually have?
answers: A buttercup is a single flower; a daisy is many tiny flowers together
Five

lessons.title: The Evening Primrose
steps: Outdoors: At dusk, sit by evening primroses and watch the buds pop open; look for moths visiting
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Evening Primrose" (p. 530) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch an evening primrose bud opening, and add the date and place
questions: When do evening primrose flowers open?
What insects carry its pollen?
answers: In the evening
Night-flying moths

lessons.title: The Hedge Bindweed
steps: Nature walk: Look along fences and hedges for bindweed vines; note which way the stem twists
Parent previews the background reading on "The Hedge Bindweed" (p. 535) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a bindweed vine twining, with its trumpet flower, and add the date and place
questions: Why does the bindweed climb other things?
Does the bindweed twine clockwise or counterclockwise?
answers: Its stem is too weak to hold itself up

lessons.title: The Dodder
steps: Go and look: In late summer, look in fields and roadsides for orange, stringy dodder tangled on other plants
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Dodder" (p. 538) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw dodder wound around a host plant; label what you can and date it
questions: How does dodder get its food?
Why doesn't dodder need green leaves?
answers: It sucks juices from the plant it twines around
It takes its food from other plants instead of making it
lessons.notes: Dodder is a parasite; just look and sketch.

lessons.title: The Milkweed
steps: Observation: Find a milkweed plant; break a leaf to see the milky sap; in fall open a pod and watch the seeds fly
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Milkweed" (p. 540) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a milkweed pod with seeds and silk; label what you can and date it
questions: What happens to milkweed's milky juice when it touches air?
How are milkweed seeds carried away?
answers: It thickens and seals the wound
By the wind, on silky parachutes
lessons.notes: Milkweed sap can irritate eyes; wash hands after breaking a leaf.

lessons.title: The White Water Lily
steps: Outdoors: At a pond, look at water lilies; notice the leaf's shape and where the stems attach
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The White Water Lily" (p. 545) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a water lily leaf and flower on the water and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Why can't the water lily live on dry land?
Where are the breathing pores on a lily pad?
answers: Its body is made for life in water; it needs its leaves floating and roots in pond mud
On the top side

lessons.title: Pondweed
steps: Nature walk: At a pond or slow stream, look under the water for pondweed and see which parts reach the surface
Parent previews the background reading on "Pondweed" (p. 548) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw pondweed under water with its flower spike above and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Where does pondweed live?
Which part comes up out of the water?
answers: Under the water
The flower spike

lessons.title: The Cat-tail
steps: Go and look: Visit a marsh and look at cat-tails; in fall pull apart a seed head and watch the fluff
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Cat-tail" (p. 551) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a cat-tail stalk with its parts; add the weather and today's date
questions: What is the brown 'cat's tail' made of?
How are cat-tail seeds scattered?
answers: Many tiny tightly packed flowers (and later seeds)
By the wind, on fluffy hairs

units.title: Unit 15: Wild Flowers III — Composite Flowers

lessons.title: A Type Lesson for a Composite Flower
steps: Observation: Pick a daisy, aster or sunflower and gently pull it apart to find the tiny flowers inside
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "A Type Lesson for a Composite Flower" (p. 554) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a ray flower and a disk flower from a composite; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: A Type Lesson for a Composite Flower (p. 554)

questions: What is a 'composite' flower?
What are the two kinds of tiny flowers in a daisy?
answers: A flower head made of many tiny flowers
Ray flowers (the 'petals') and disk flowers (the center)

lessons.title: The Goldenrod
steps: Outdoors: In late summer, look at goldenrod; count the insects visiting one plant
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Goldenrod" (p. 555) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a goldenrod plume and one flower head, and add the date and place
questions: Why are goldenrod flower heads crowded together?
Name a kind of insect you saw on goldenrod.
answers: They are tiny, so many together make a big show that insects notice

lessons.title: The Asters
steps: Nature walk: In fall, find asters along roadsides and compare the colors and sizes of different kinds
Parent previews the background reading on "The Asters" (p. 558) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch an aster flower head, and add the date and place
questions: How is an aster built like a sunflower?
When do asters bloom?
answers: It has a center of disk flowers surrounded by ray flowers
In late summer and fall

lessons.title: The White Daisy and the Black-eyed Susan
steps: Go and look: Find a white daisy and a black-eyed Susan; take each apart and compare them
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The White Daisy and the Black-eyed Susan" (p. 560) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a daisy and a black-eyed Susan side by side; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Yellow Daisy or Black-eyed Susan (p. 562)

questions: What color are the centers of the white daisy and the black-eyed Susan?
Is a daisy one flower or many?
answers: Yellow for the daisy, dark brown for the black-eyed Susan
Many tiny flowers

lessons.title: The Thistle
steps: Observation: Find a thistle; look (carefully!) at its spines and at bees on the purple flower head
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Thistle" (p. 563) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a thistle head and a spiny leaf; label what you can and date it
questions: What do a thistle's spines do?
How do thistle seeds travel?
answers: Keep grazing animals from eating it
On fluffy down carried by the wind

lessons.title: The Burdock
steps: Outdoors: Find burdock in a waste place; in fall, see what happens when burrs touch your sleeve
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Burdock" (p. 566) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a burr's hooks and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does burdock spread its seeds?
How does burdock crowd out other plants?
answers: Its hooked burrs stick to animals and clothes
Its huge leaves shade them

lessons.title: Prickly Lettuce, A Compass Plant
steps: Nature walk: Find prickly lettuce on a roadside and look at which way its leaves face
Parent previews the background reading on "Prickly Lettuce, A Compass Plant" (p. 570) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a prickly lettuce plant showing its edge-on leaves and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: Prickly Lettuce, A Compass Plant (p. 570)

questions: Why is it called a compass plant?
Why does the plant turn its leaves edge-on?
answers: Its leaves turn edgewise north and south
To avoid the hot midday sun

lessons.title: The Dandelion
steps: Go and look: Find dandelions; look at a flower, a closed head and a seed puff, and blow the seeds away
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Dandelion" (p. 572) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a dandelion through its stages, flower to puffball; add the weather and today's date
questions: How do dandelion seeds travel?
Why is it hard to pull a dandelion out?
answers: By the wind on little parachutes
It has a long taproot that breaks off and grows again

units.title: Unit 16: Wild Flowers IV — Everlasting to Weeds

lessons.title: The Pearly Everlasting
steps: Observation: In a dry pasture or roadside, look for whitish woolly plants with papery white flowers
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Pearly Everlasting" (p. 576) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch pearly everlasting flowers; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why is it called everlasting?
What protects its leaves?
answers: Its dry papery flowers keep their look a long time
A woolly coat

lessons.title: The Jewelweed, or Touch-me-not
steps: Outdoors: In a damp shady place, find jewelweed; touch a ripe pod and watch it burst; dip a leaf in water
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Jewelweed, or Touch-me-not" (p. 578) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a jewelweed pod before and after bursting, and add the date and place
questions: Why is it called touch-me-not?
What happens when you hold a jewelweed leaf under water?
answers: Its ripe pods burst when touched
It looks silvery
lessons.notes: Jewelweed often grows near poison ivy; know what poison ivy looks like before you go.

lessons.title: Mullein
steps: Nature walk: Find a mullein plant in a dry field; feel its leaves and look at the tall flower spike
Parent previews the background reading on "Mullein" (p. 582) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a mullein rosette and flower stalk, and add the date and place
questions: Why are mullein leaves soft and woolly?
How long does a mullein plant take to bloom?
answers: The felt keeps in water and stops animals from grazing
Two years (rosette the first year, flower stalk the second)

lessons.title: The Teasel
steps: Go and look: Find a teasel along a roadside; look at how rain collects where the leaves join the stem
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Teasel" (p. 586) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a teasel head; label what you can and date it
questions: What was teasel used for?
What collects in the cups made by its leaves?
answers: Raising the nap on woolen cloth
Rainwater (which traps insects)

lessons.title: Queen Anne’s Lace, or Wild Carrot
steps: Observation: Find Queen Anne's lace; look for the one dark purple flower in the center; watch a flower head close into a 'bird's nest'
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Queen Anne’s Lace, or Wild Carrot" (p. 589) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw Queen Anne's lace, open and closed; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: Queen Anne’s Lace, or Wild Carrot (p. 589)

questions: Where did Queen Anne's lace come from?
What garden plant is Queen Anne's lace related to?
answers: Europe
The carrot

lessons.title: Weeds, with an Outline for Studying One
steps: Outdoors: Pick one weed in your yard and study it: where it grows, its root and how it spreads its seed
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Weeds, with an Outline for Studying One" (p. 594) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw the whole weed, roots and all and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: Outline for the Study of a Weed (p. 595)

questions: What is a weed?
Is a plant a weed everywhere it grows?
answers: A plant growing where we do not want it
No; it depends on where it is

units.title: Unit 17: Cultivated Plants I — Garden Flowers

lessons.title: The Crocus
steps: Nature walk: In early spring, look for crocuses in gardens; dig one up (with permission) or cut one in half to see the corm
Parent previews the background reading on "The Crocus" (p. 596) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a crocus plant with its corm and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Why can crocuses bloom so early?
Do crocuses grow from bulbs or corms?
answers: They use food stored underground from last year
Corms

lessons.title: Daffodils and their Relatives
steps: Go and look: Look at daffodils and narcissus in gardens; compare the size of each flower's trumpet
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Daffodils and their Relatives" (p. 599) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a daffodil showing its trumpet and petals; add the weather and today's date
questions: What do daffodils grow from?
When should daffodil bulbs be planted?
answers: Bulbs
In the fall

lessons.title: The Tulip
steps: Observation: Look at tulips in a garden; notice how the flowers open in sun and close at night
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Tulip" (p. 603) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a tulip and its bulb; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why can tulips bloom so early in spring?
Do tulip flowers close at night?
answers: Food stored in the bulb the year before
Yes

lessons.title: The Pansy
steps: Outdoors: Look at pansies in a garden bed; find the 'face' on each flower
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Pansy" (p. 607) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a pansy face, and add the date and place
questions: What wild flower family does the pansy belong to?
What does a pansy's 'face' help the plant do?
answers: The violet family
Attract insects

lessons.title: The Bleeding Heart
steps: Nature walk: Find a bleeding heart plant; gently open a flower to see its double swing doors
Parent previews the background reading on "The Bleeding Heart" (p. 611) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a bleeding heart flower row, and add the date and place
questions: How does a bee reach the bleeding heart's nectar?
What shape is the flower?
answers: It pushes open the inner petals like swinging doors
A heart

lessons.title: Poppies
steps: Go and look: Look at poppies in a garden; find buds, open flowers and seed pods
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Poppies" (p. 613) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a poppy seed capsule with its holes; label what you can and date it
questions: What happens to the poppy's sepals when the flower opens?
How do poppy seeds get out of the pod?
answers: They fall off
Through little holes under the cap, shaken out by the wind

lessons.title: The California Poppy
steps: Observation: If you can, find California poppies; watch them close on cloudy days and at night
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The California Poppy" (p. 616) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a California poppy; label what you can and date it
questions: Where is the California poppy native?
What does it do in cloudy weather?
answers: California
Closes its flower

lessons.title: The Nasturtium
steps: Outdoors: Look at nasturtiums in a garden; find the spur and watch how the stamens move over a few days
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Nasturtium" (p. 620) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a nasturtium with its spur and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Where does a nasturtium keep its nectar?
Can you eat nasturtium leaves?
answers: In the long spur
Yes; they taste peppery

lessons.title: The Bee-Larkspur
steps: Nature walk: Watch a larkspur plant; see which insects visit the flowers and how they reach in
Parent previews the background reading on "The Bee-Larkspur" (p. 623) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a larkspur flower with its spur and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Where does the larkspur's flower stalk add new buds?
What insect gets the nectar from deep inside?
answers: At its tip, all summer long
Bumblebees

lessons.title: The Blue Flag, or Iris
steps: Go and look: Find an iris (blue flag) in a garden or wet meadow; look for the three 'doors' to the nectar
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Blue Flag, or Iris" (p. 626) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch an iris with its three drooping and three upright parts; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: The Blue Flag, or Iris (p. 626)

questions: How many entrances to the nectar does an iris flower have?
What does a bee brush against as it enters?
answers: Three
The pollen and stigma

lessons.title: The Sunflower
steps: Observation: Grow or find a sunflower; watch the florets open in rings from the outside in; check the seeds in fall
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Sunflower" (p. 631) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch the spiral pattern of sunflower seeds; add the weather and today's date
questions: Is a sunflower one flower?
In which direction do the florets open?
answers: No; it is a large family of tiny florets
From the outside toward the center

units.title: Unit 18: Cultivated Plants II — Garden Flowers, Clovers and Crops

lessons.title: The Bachelor’s Button
steps: Outdoors: Find a bachelor's button (cornflower); pull it apart to see the separate little flowers
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Bachelor’s Button" (p. 636) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch one floret of a bachelor's button, and add the date and place
questions: Is a bachelor's button one flower or many?
answers: Many little flowers together

lessons.title: The Salvia or Scarlet Sage
steps: Nature walk: Look at scarlet sage in a garden; see which parts are red; watch for hummingbirds
Parent previews the background reading on "The Salvia or Scarlet Sage" (p. 637) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a salvia flower with its red calyx, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Salvia or Scarlet Sage (p. 637)

questions: Which parts of the salvia are red?
What bird often visits salvia?
answers: The bracts, calyx and flower, not just the petals
The hummingbird

lessons.title: Petunias
steps: Go and look: Look at petunias in a garden or pot; smell them in the evening; look for night moths
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Petunias" (p. 640) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a petunia flower trumpet; label what you can and date it
questions: Where did petunias first come from?
When are petunias most fragrant?
answers: South America
In the evening

lessons.title: The Horseshoe Geranium
steps: Observation: Look at a geranium in a pot; feel and smell its leaves and find the horseshoe mark
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Horseshoe Geranium" (p. 643) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a geranium leaf with its horseshoe band; label what you can and date it
questions: Why is it called a horseshoe geranium?
Why are geraniums good for flower beds?
answers: Its leaves have a dark horseshoe-shaped band
They bloom a long time and do well in sun

lessons.title: The Sweet Pea
steps: Outdoors: Look at sweet peas (or garden peas) climbing; find the tendrils and a pod
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Sweet Pea" (p. 649) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a sweet pea tendril and flower and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What are the sweet pea's tendrils?
What other plant has a flower shaped like the sweet pea's?
answers: Leaflets changed into curling holdfasts
The clover (and garden pea and bean)

lessons.title: The Clovers
steps: Nature walk: Find red clover; pull a floret and taste the nectar at the base; watch bumblebees on it
Parent previews the background reading on "The Clovers" (p. 652) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a clover head and leaf and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How do clovers help the soil?
Which bee pollinates red clover best?
answers: They add nitrogen to it
The bumblebee

lessons.title: Sweet Clover
steps: Go and look: Look for sweet clover (white or yellow) on roadsides; smell its flowers and crushed leaves
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Sweet Clover" (p. 655) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a sweet clover stem; add the weather and today's date
questions: Where does sweet clover grow well?
How does it make poor soil better?
answers: In poor soil where other plants struggle
Its roots add nitrogen and let in air

lessons.title: The White Clover
steps: Observation: In a lawn, look for white clover; follow a creeping stem; watch honey bees visit
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The White Clover" (p. 658) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a white clover plant with its creeping stem; add the weather and today's date
questions: How does white clover spread?
Which insect depends on white clover for honey?
answers: By creeping stems that root as they go
The honey bee

lessons.title: Maize, or Indian Corn
steps: Outdoors: Look at a cornfield or garden corn; find the tassel, silks and ears
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Maize, or Indian Corn" (p. 660) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a corn plant with tassel, silk and ear, and add the date and place
questions: Where is corn pollen made?
What are corn silks for?
answers: In the tassel at the top
Each silk catches pollen for one kernel

lessons.title: The Cotton Plant
steps: Nature walk: If you can't see a cotton field, look at a cotton ball and cotton cloth closely with a lens
Parent previews the background reading on "The Cotton Plant" (p. 666) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a cotton boll opening, and add the date and place
questions: What part of the cotton plant do we use for cloth?
answers: The fibers attached to the seeds in the boll

lessons.title: The Strawberry
steps: Go and look: Find strawberry plants; look for runners and count the seeds on a berry
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Strawberry" (p. 672) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a strawberry plant with a runner; label what you can and date it
questions: Where are a strawberry's seeds?
What are the two ways a strawberry plant makes new plants?
answers: On the outside of the berry
Seeds and runners

lessons.title: The Pumpkin
steps: Observation: Look at pumpkin or squash vines in a garden or patch; find male and female flowers and the tendrils
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Pumpkin" (p. 675) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a pumpkin flower and a baby pumpkin under it; label what you can and date it
questions: Who grew pumpkins and squash long before Columbus?
How can you tell a female pumpkin flower?
answers: American Indians, in their cornfields
It has a tiny pumpkin at its base

units.title: Unit 19: Flowerless Plants — Ferns, Mosses, Fungi and Bacteria

lessons.title: The Christmas Fern
steps: Outdoors: In woods any time of year, find Christmas fern; look under the fronds for spore dots
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Christmas Fern" (p. 684) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw one Christmas fern leaflet with its 'boot' shape and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Why is it called the Christmas fern?
What shape is each leaflet?
answers: It stays green all winter, at Christmas time
Like a little boot or stocking

lessons.title: The Bracken
steps: Nature walk: Look in open woods and clearings for bracken, a large three-parted fern
Parent previews the background reading on "The Bracken" (p. 689) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a bracken frond showing its three parts and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Where does bracken grow?
How does bracken spread?
answers: Almost all over the world, in open woods and clearings
By underground stems

lessons.title: How a Fern Bud Unfolds
steps: Go and look: In spring, find fern 'fiddleheads' and visit them every few days to see them unroll
Parent reads the teacher's background for "How a Fern Bud Unfolds" (p. 691) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a fiddlehead uncurling, in three stages; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: How a Fern Bud Unfolds (p. 691)

questions: What is a young fern bud called?
How are the parts of a fern frond packed inside the bud?
answers: A fiddlehead
Rolled up in a tight spiral

lessons.title: The Fruiting of the Fern
steps: Observation: Turn over fern fronds and look for brown dots; tap one over white paper to see the spore dust
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Fruiting of the Fern" (p. 693) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch the brown spore dots under a fern leaflet; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: The Fruiting of the Fern (p. 693)

questions: Do ferns have flowers and seeds?
Where are spores made on most ferns?
answers: No; they make spores
In brown dots on the underside of the fronds

lessons.title: The Field Horsetail
steps: Outdoors: In April or May, look in sandy fields and railroad banks for horsetail's pale fertile stems, then green stems later
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Field Horsetail" (p. 699) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a green horsetail stem with its whorls, and add the date and place
questions: What does a horsetail have instead of leaves?
Does a horsetail grow from seeds?
answers: Green jointed stems that do the work of leaves
No; from spores

lessons.title: The Hair-cap Moss, or Pigeon Wheat
steps: Nature walk: Find a patch of hair-cap moss; look for the spore capsules on tall stalks
Parent previews the background reading on "The Hair-cap Moss, or Pigeon Wheat" (p. 702) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a moss plant with its capsule and cap, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Hair-cap Moss, or Pigeon Wheat (p. 702)

questions: How does a moss make new plants?
What is moss's 'hair cap'?
answers: By spores from its capsules
A hairy hood covering the spore capsule

lessons.title: Mushrooms and other Fungi
steps: Go and look: After a rain, look for mushrooms in a lawn or woods (never taste them); place a cap on paper overnight for a spore print
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Mushrooms and other Fungi" (p. 706) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a mushroom with cap, gills and stem labeled; label what you can and date it
questions: What part of the fungus is the mushroom?
Is it safe to eat wild mushrooms you find?
answers: The fruiting part; the main fungus is a mass of threads underground
No; many are poisonous, so never taste one
lessons.notes: Never eat or taste any wild mushroom; some deadly ones look harmless. Wash hands after touching.

lessons.title: Puffballs
steps: Observation: Look for puffballs in fields or woods; squeeze a ripe one to see the 'smoke' of spores
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Puffballs" (p. 712) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a puffball letting out its spore cloud; label what you can and date it
questions: What is the 'smoke' that comes out of a ripe puffball?
answers: Millions of spores

lessons.title: The Bracket Fungi
steps: Outdoors: Look on dead trees, logs and stumps for shelf-shaped bracket fungi; check underneath for tiny pores
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Bracket Fungi" (p. 714) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a bracket fungus on a stump and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Why are bracket fungi bad for trees?
Where does a bracket fungus release its spores?
answers: Their threads rot the wood inside the tree
From tiny pores on its underside

lessons.title: Hedgehog Fungi, Scarlet Saucer, Morels and Stinkhorns
steps: Nature walk: On a woods walk, look for unusual fungi: toothed hedgehogs, red cups in early spring, honeycomb-capped morels (look only)
Parent previews the background reading on "Hedgehog Fungi, Scarlet Saucer, Morels and Stinkhorns" (p. 717) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw the strangest fungus you found and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What color is the scarlet saucer?
What does a morel's cap look like?
answers: Bright red
A sponge or honeycomb
lessons.notes: The stinkhorns smell awful; Comstock herself says to skip a live lesson on them.

lessons.title: Molds
steps: Go and look: Leave a slice of bread in a closed bag for a week (don't open it) and watch mold grow
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Molds" (p. 720) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the mold patches and their colors; add the weather and today's date
questions: Where do mold spores come from?
What do molds need to grow?
answers: They are everywhere in the air and dust
Food, moisture and warmth
lessons.notes: Keep the moldy bread sealed and throw it away unopened; mold spores can bother allergies.

lessons.title: Bacteria
steps: Observation: Wash hands, then touch a slice of potato or gelatin; seal it in a jar and watch for spots that grow over days
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Bacteria" (p. 723) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch what grew on your test; add the weather and today's date
questions: Can we see a single bacterium with our eyes alone?
Why should we wash our hands before eating?
answers: No; we need a microscope
To remove bacteria (germs) that can make us sick
lessons.notes: Throw the test away sealed when you're done; don't open it to sniff.

units.title: Unit 20: Tree Study I — How Trees Grow, and Shade and Nut Trees

lessons.title: How a Tree Grows
steps: Outdoors: Look at a tree stump and count its rings; look at twigs for buds and leaf scars
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "How a Tree Grows" (p. 726) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a stump's rings, and add the date and place
questions: What does each ring in a tree trunk stand for?
Where does a tree grow new wood?
answers: One year of growth
In a thin layer just under the bark

lessons.title: How to Begin Tree Study
steps: Nature walk: Adopt a tree near your home: visit it in each season and record its shape, bark, leaves and fruit
Parent previews the background reading on "How to Begin Tree Study" (p. 731) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch the whole outline of your tree, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: How to Begin Tree Study (p. 731)

questions: How does the book suggest starting tree study?
answers: Pick a tree and watch it all year, beginning with its leaves and fruit in the fall

lessons.title: How to Make Leaf Prints
steps: Go and look: Collect leaves from different trees and make leaf prints with paint, ink, or crayon rubbings
Parent reads the teacher's background for "How to Make Leaf Prints" (p. 734) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a print of each leaf with its tree's name; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: How to Make Leaf Prints (p. 734)

questions: What is a leaf print?
answers: A picture made by inking or rubbing a leaf so it prints its shape and veins

lessons.title: The Maples
steps: Observation: Find a maple; look at its leaf shape, its paired winged seeds and, in fall, its colors
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Maples" (p. 736) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a maple leaf and a pair of winged seeds; label what you can and date it
questions: What sweet food comes from sugar maple sap?
How do maple seeds travel?
answers: Maple syrup and maple sugar
They spin on wings in the wind

lessons.title: The American Elm
steps: Outdoors: Find an elm (many were lost to disease) and notice its vase shape; feel its rough, lopsided leaves
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The American Elm" (p. 745) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw the vase shape of an elm and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What shape does an American elm make?
Is the base of an elm leaf even or lopsided?
answers: A graceful vase or fountain
Lopsided
lessons.notes: Dutch elm disease killed many American elms after 1930; a park or campus is a good place to look.

lessons.title: The Oak
steps: Nature walk: Find an oak tree; collect acorns and compare leaves with rounded lobes and pointed lobes
Parent previews the background reading on "The Oak" (p. 748) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw an acorn and an oak leaf and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What is the oak's fruit called?
What does the oak stand for?
answers: An acorn
Strength and loyalty

lessons.title: The Shagbark Hickory
steps: Go and look: Look for a shagbark hickory with its long, curling strips of bark; look for nuts underneath in fall
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Shagbark Hickory" (p. 755) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a strip of shagbark bark and a hickory leaf; add the weather and today's date
questions: Why is it called shagbark?
Are hickory leaves simple or compound?
answers: Its bark peels in long shaggy strips
Compound

lessons.title: The Chestnut
steps: Observation: Find a chestnut tree if you can (most American chestnuts died of blight); look at the burs and nuts
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Chestnut" (p. 757) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a chestnut bur; add the weather and today's date
questions: What protects the chestnuts on the tree?
What happened to most American chestnut trees?
answers: A prickly bur
They were killed by the chestnut blight (a fungus)
lessons.notes: Most American chestnuts died of blight after 1904; you may need to look at a photo or a Chinese chestnut instead.

lessons.title: The Horse-Chestnut
steps: Outdoors: Find a horse-chestnut (buckeye) tree; look at its big sticky buds in winter and its spiny fruits in fall
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Horse-Chestnut" (p. 761) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a horse-chestnut leaf with its leaflets, and add the date and place
questions: How many leaflets does a horse-chestnut leaf have?
Can people eat horse-chestnuts?
answers: Five to seven, spread like fingers
No; they are poisonous
lessons.notes: Horse-chestnuts are poisonous; don't mix them up with edible chestnuts.

lessons.title: The Willows
steps: Nature walk: Look along streams for willows; in early spring find the soft 'pussy willow' catkins
Parent previews the background reading on "The Willows" (p. 765) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a pussy willow twig, and add the date and place
questions: Do willows have pollen flowers and seed flowers on the same tree?
Where do willows like to grow?
answers: No; they are on separate trees
In wet places, near water

lessons.title: The Cottonwood or Carolina Poplar
steps: Go and look: Find a cottonwood or poplar; in early summer look for drifting 'cotton'; listen to the leaves rattle in the wind
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Cottonwood or Carolina Poplar" (p. 770) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a cottonwood leaf with its flat stem; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Cottonwood or Carolina Poplar (p. 770)

questions: What is the 'cotton' that floats from the tree?
Why do poplar leaves shake in a light breeze?
answers: Fluff that carries its seeds
Their leaf stems are flat

lessons.title: The White Ash
steps: Observation: Find a white ash; notice its compound leaves in pairs and its paddle-shaped seeds
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The White Ash" (p. 774) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw an ash leaf and its seeds; label what you can and date it
questions: Name something made from ash wood.
How are ash leaves and twigs arranged?
answers: Baseball bats, tool handles, oars, furniture
In opposite pairs

units.title: Unit 21: Tree Study II — Apples, Evergreens and Flowering Shrubs

lessons.title: The Apple Tree
steps: Outdoors: Visit an apple tree; look at its shape, bark and twigs with fruit spurs
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Apple Tree" (p. 778) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw the outline of an apple tree and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How are new apple trees of a certain kind usually made?
Does every variety of apple tree have its own shape?
answers: By grafting or budding, not from seed
Yes

lessons.title: How an Apple Grows
steps: Nature walk: In spring, look at apple blossoms; later, visit the same branch to watch tiny apples form
Parent previews the background reading on "How an Apple Grows" (p. 782) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw an apple blossom and a tiny apple and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What is the purpose of the apple blossom?
Which part of the blossom becomes the apple?
answers: To make apples with seeds
The base of the flower around the seed-chambers (the ovary area)

lessons.title: The Apple
steps: Go and look: Cut an apple across its middle and look for the star; compare two kinds of apples by taste and look
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Apple" (p. 785) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the star pattern in a cut apple; add the weather and today's date
questions: What shape do the seed chambers make in an apple cut crosswise?
How many seed chambers are there?
answers: A five-pointed star
Five

lessons.title: The Pine
steps: Observation: Find a pine; count the needles in a bundle; collect a cone and look for seeds
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Pine" (p. 789) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a pine needle bundle and a cone; add the weather and today's date
questions: Do pines lose all their needles in the fall?
Where are pine seeds?
answers: No; they shed them a few at a time
Under the scales of the cones

lessons.title: The Norway Spruce
steps: Outdoors: Find a spruce; feel its square needles and compare its hanging cones with pine cones
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Norway Spruce" (p. 796) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch a spruce twig and hanging cone, and add the date and place
questions: Where did the Norway spruce come from?
Do spruce cones point up or hang down?
answers: Europe
Hang down

lessons.title: The Hemlock
steps: Nature walk: Find a hemlock; look at the two white lines under each flat needle and its tiny cones
Parent previews the background reading on "The Hemlock" (p. 801) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch a hemlock twig from below, and add the date and place
questions: How can you know a hemlock needle?
Why is a hemlock grove good shelter in winter?
answers: It is short and flat with two white lines underneath
Its thick evergreen branches block wind and snow

lessons.title: The Flowering Dogwood
steps: Go and look: In spring, find flowering dogwood; look closely at the white 'petals' and the tiny true flowers in the middle
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Flowering Dogwood" (p. 803) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a dogwood blossom with its four bracts; label what you can and date it
questions: Are the four white 'petals' of a dogwood really petals?
answers: No; they are bracts around a cluster of tiny flowers

lessons.title: The Staghorn Sumac
steps: Observation: Find staghorn sumac at a roadside or field edge; feel its velvety twigs; see its red fruit clusters
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Staghorn Sumac" (p. 806) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a sumac branch with its fruit cone; label what you can and date it
questions: Why is it called staghorn sumac?
What color do sumac leaves turn in fall?
answers: Its velvety branches look like a deer's antlers in velvet
Bright red

lessons.title: The Witch-Hazel
steps: Outdoors: In late fall, look for witch-hazel blooming with yellow ribbon petals; look for its shooting seed pods
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Witch-Hazel" (p. 810) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a witch-hazel flower and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: When does witch-hazel bloom?
How does witch-hazel scatter its seeds?
answers: In the autumn
Its pods snap open and shoot them out

lessons.title: The Mountain Laurel
steps: Nature walk: In early summer, find mountain laurel in bloom; gently touch a stamen with a grass stem and watch it spring
Parent previews the background reading on "The Mountain Laurel" (p. 813) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a laurel flower with its ten springs and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How many spring-like stamens does a laurel flower have?
What do the springs do?
answers: Ten
Flick pollen onto visiting insects
lessons.notes: Mountain laurel leaves are poisonous; look and touch gently, but don't chew.

units.title: Unit 22: Earth Study I — Brooks, Crystals and Minerals

lessons.title: The Brook
steps: Go and look: Visit a brook and watch where the water runs fast and slow; drop a leaf in and follow it
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Brook" (p. 818) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a map of the brook's bends; add the weather and today's date
questions: Where is all brook water finally going?
What does running water carry along?
answers: Toward the ocean
Soil, sand and stones

lessons.title: How a Brook Drops its Load
steps: Observation: Shake soil and water in a jar and watch the layers settle; at a brook, look where sand and gravel collect
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "How a Brook Drops its Load" (p. 822) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch the layers in your jar; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: How a Brook Drops its Load (p. 822)

questions: When does a brook drop its load?
Which settles first, big stones or fine mud?
answers: When its current slows down
Big stones

lessons.title: Crystal Growth
steps: Outdoors: Dissolve sugar or alum in hot water and hang a string in it; check for crystals over several days
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Crystal Growth" (p. 825) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch the crystals that grew, and add the date and place
questions: How are crystals made from a solution?
Does each substance make crystals of its own shape?
answers: As the water evaporates, the substance forms crystals
Yes
lessons.notes: Use hot water with a parent's help.

lessons.title: Salt
steps: Nature walk: Dissolve salt in water in a saucer and let it dry in the sun; look at the crystals with a lens
Parent previews the background reading on "Salt" (p. 827) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch salt crystals, and add the date and place
questions: What shape are salt crystals?
Where does salt come from?
answers: Cubes
Seawater, salt springs, and mines

lessons.title: How to Study Minerals
steps: Go and look: Collect a few different pebbles and stones; sort them by color, hardness and how they feel
Parent reads the teacher's background for "How to Study Minerals" (p. 828) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw your stone collection with labels; label what you can and date it
questions: Name one way to sort stones.
answers: By color, hardness, weight, or whether they sparkle

lessons.title: Quartz
steps: Observation: Look for quartz in pebbles and rocks: glassy or milky stones; test if it scratches glass (with a parent)
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Quartz" (p. 829) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw a quartz crystal with its six sides; label what you can and date it
questions: How many sides does a quartz crystal have?
Can quartz scratch glass?
answers: Six
Yes

lessons.title: Feldspar
steps: Outdoors: Look at a piece of granite for pinkish or white blocky grains of feldspar
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "Feldspar" (p. 831) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a feldspar grain and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Which is more common, feldspar or quartz?
answers: Feldspar

lessons.title: Mica
steps: Nature walk: Find mica in a rock or sand; peel off thin flakes with a fingernail
Parent previews the background reading on "Mica" (p. 832) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a stack of mica flakes and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How does mica break?
answers: Into thin, clear, flexible sheets

lessons.title: Granite
steps: Go and look: Look at granite (countertops, curbs, gravestones) with a lens and find its three minerals
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Granite" (p. 833) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch a magnified piece of granite; add the weather and today's date
questions: What three minerals make up granite?
answers: Feldspar, quartz and mica

lessons.title: Calcite, marble and Limestone
steps: Observation: Drop a little vinegar on limestone, marble or chalk and watch it fizz
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Calcite, marble and Limestone" (p. 835) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a calcite crystal or fizzing chalk; add the weather and today's date
questions: What happens when vinegar touches limestone?
What rock forms when limestone is changed by heat and pressure?
answers: It fizzes, giving off gas
Marble
lessons.notes: Comstock uses stronger acid; plain vinegar is safe and works.

units.title: Unit 23: Earth Study II — Magnets, Soil, Water and Weather

lessons.title: The Magnet
steps: Outdoors: Test what a magnet picks up around the house; float a magnetized needle on a cork and see which way it points
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Magnet" (p. 838) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch what the magnet picked up, and add the date and place
questions: What metal does a magnet attract?
Which way does a free-turning magnet point?
answers: Iron (and steel)
North and south

lessons.title: The Soil
steps: Nature walk: Dig a small hole and look at the soil layers; feel soil from a garden and from a sandy or clay spot
Parent previews the background reading on "The Soil" (p. 842) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch the layers in your hole, and add the date and place
questions: What two things make up soil?
Why must soil be porous?
answers: Rock flour (broken-down rock) and humus (decayed plants and animals)
So roots can get air and water

lessons.title: Water Forms
steps: Go and look: Watch water in different forms: breath fog on a cold window, dew on grass, frost, ice, snowflakes on dark cloth
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Water Forms" (p. 850) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw a snowflake or frost pattern; label what you can and date it
questions: How many points does a snowflake usually have?
What is dew?
answers: Six
Water vapor from the air that condenses on cool surfaces

lessons.title: The Weather, part 1: History and the Atmosphere
steps: Observation: Start a weather notebook: each day record the sky, wind, temperature and rain or snow
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "History and the Atmosphere" (p. 857) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw today's sky and a weather symbol; label what you can and date it
questions: What surrounds the earth like an ocean of air?
What did you notice about today's weather?
answers: The atmosphere
lessons.notes: The weather chapter was written by Wilford M. Wilson of the U.S. Weather Bureau; some numbers and methods are from 1911.

lessons.title: The Weather, part 2: The Winds of the World
steps: Outdoors: Watch which way the wind blows each day this week using a streamer or flag; notice how the weather changes with the wind
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Winds of the World" (p. 866) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw a wind direction chart for the week and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What makes the wind blow?
From which direction did the wind blow most this week?
answers: Uneven heating of the air, which causes differences in air pressure

lessons.title: The Weather, part 3: Storms, Weather Maps and the Weather Service
steps: Nature walk: Before and during a storm, watch the clouds and wind; compare with today's weather map online or in a newspaper
Parent previews the background reading on "Storms, Weather Maps and the Weather Service" (p. 874) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw a weather map with a high and a low and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: What weather does a 'low' on a weather map usually bring?
Why is a weather service useful?
answers: Clouds and storms
It warns people of storms and helps farmers and sailors plan

lessons.title: Experiments to Show Air Pressure
steps: Go and look: Do the air pressure experiment: fill a glass to the brim, cover with a card, turn it over over a sink
Parent reads the teacher's background for "Experiments to Show Air Pressure" (p. 877) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch the upside-down glass and card; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: Experiments to Show Air Pressure (p. 877)

questions: Why doesn't the water fall out of the upside-down glass?
In which directions does air press?
answers: Air pressing up on the card holds it in
In all directions equally

lessons.title: The Barometer
steps: Observation: Look at a barometer (or a weather app) each day and note whether pressure is rising or falling
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Barometer" (p. 878) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch a barometer dial; add the weather and today's date
questions: What does a barometer measure?
What does falling air pressure often mean?
answers: Air pressure
Stormy weather is coming

lessons.title: How to read Weather Maps
steps: Outdoors: Find today's weather map; locate your home and the nearest high and low
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "How to read Weather Maps" (p. 879) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch today's weather map with arrows for wind, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: How to read Weather Maps (p. 879)

questions: What are isobars?
Which way does weather usually move across the United States?
answers: Lines on a map joining places with the same air pressure
From west to east

units.title: Unit 24: Sky Study I — The Stars

lessons.title: The Story of the Stars
steps: Nature walk: On a clear night, go outside with a blanket and just look at the stars for ten minutes
Parent previews the background reading on "The Story of the Stars" (p. 887) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch the brightest stars you saw, and add the date and place

links.label: Read: The Story of the Stars (p. 887)

questions: Why does the author wish she had learned the constellations as a child?
answers: So she could feel at home among the stars

lessons.title: How to Begin Star Study
steps: Go and look: On a clear evening, find the Big Dipper and use the two pointer stars to find the North Star
Parent reads the teacher's background for "How to Begin Star Study" (p. 889) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw the Big Dipper, its pointers and the North Star; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: How to Begin Star Study (p. 889)

questions: How can you find the North Star?
What constellation is the North Star in?
answers: Follow the two pointer stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl
The Little Dipper

lessons.title: Cassiopeia’s Chair, Cepheus and the Dragon
steps: Observation: On a clear night, find Cassiopeia's 'W' on the opposite side of the North Star from the Big Dipper
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Cassiopeia’s Chair, Cepheus and the Dragon" (p. 893) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw Cassiopeia, the North Star and the Big Dipper; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: Cassiopeia’s Chair, Cepheus and the Dragon (p. 893)

questions: What shape does Cassiopeia's Chair make?
Why do these star groups never set for us?
answers: A W (or M)
They are close to the North Star and circle around it

lessons.title: The Winter Stars and Orion
steps: Outdoors: On a winter evening, find Orion and his three-star belt
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Winter Stars and Orion" (p. 895) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw Orion with his belt and sword and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How do you know Orion?
What color is the bright star Betelgeuse in Orion?
answers: By the three bright stars in a row that make his belt
Reddish

lessons.title: Aldebaran and the Pleiades
steps: Nature walk: On a winter evening, follow Orion's belt up to red Aldebaran, then on to the little cluster of the Pleiades
Parent previews the background reading on "Aldebaran and the Pleiades" (p. 897) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw Aldebaran and the Pleiades and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: How many stars can most people see in the Pleiades?
Are there really more?
answers: About six or seven
Yes, many more that we cannot see without a telescope

lessons.title: The Two Dog-Stars, Sirius and Procyon
steps: Go and look: Follow Orion's belt down to Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky; then find Procyon
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Two Dog-Stars, Sirius and Procyon" (p. 898) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Nature journal: sketch Orion, Sirius and Procyon; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: The Two Dog-Stars, Sirius and Procyon (p. 898)

questions: Which star is the brightest in the night sky?
How can you find Sirius?
answers: Sirius, the Dog Star
Follow Orion's belt downward

lessons.title: Capella and the Heavenly Twins
steps: Observation: On a winter evening, look high overhead for bright Capella and the twin stars Castor and Pollux
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "Capella and the Heavenly Twins" (p. 900) and shares what you saw together
Nature journal: sketch Capella and the Twins; add the weather and today's date

links.label: Read: Capella and the Heavenly Twins (p. 900)

questions: What are the names of the two bright Twin stars?
answers: Castor and Pollux

lessons.title: The Stars of Summer
steps: Outdoors: On a summer evening, find the Summer Triangle (Vega, Deneb, Altair) and the Milky Way if skies are dark
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "The Stars of Summer" (p. 901) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: sketch the Summer Triangle, and add the date and place
questions: Are the stars we see in summer the same as winter?
What is the Milky Way?
answers: No, except those near the North Star
A band of countless faraway stars

units.title: Unit 25: Sky Study II — The Sun and the Moon

lessons.title: The Sun
steps: Nature walk: Watch the sunrise or sunset and notice where on the horizon it happens; mark the spot and check again in a month (never look straight at the sun)
Parent previews the background reading on "The Sun" (p. 905) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: sketch the horizon with the sun's setting point, and add the date and place
questions: Where do we get our light and heat?
Is the sun a star?
answers: From the sun
Yes
lessons.notes: Never look straight at the sun, even through sunglasses.

lessons.title: The Tropic of Cancer and the Garden; the Zodiac
steps: Go and look: Read the short story about the Tropic of Cancer together, then note on a calendar the longest and shortest days of the year
Parent reads the teacher's background for "The Tropic of Cancer and the Garden; the Zodiac" (p. 909) and reads a favorite paragraph aloud
Journal page: draw the sun's high summer path and low winter path; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Relation between the Tropic of Cancer and the Planting of the Garden (p. 909)
Read: The Zodiac and its Signs (p. 911)

questions: What is the Tropic of Cancer?
How many signs are in the zodiac?
answers: The farthest line north where the sun is ever directly overhead (in June)
Twelve
lessons.notes: Comstock treats the zodiac as old sky lore and calendar history, not as fortune-telling.

lessons.title: The Relations of the Sun to the Earth
steps: Observation: At noon on a sunny day, measure the length of a stick's shadow; repeat each month
Before or after the outing, a parent reads Comstock's notes on "The Relations of the Sun to the Earth" (p. 913) and shares what you saw together
Journal page: draw the noon shadow length each month; label what you can and date it

links.label: Read: The Relations of the Sun to the Earth (p. 913)

questions: When is the sun highest in the sky at noon?
Why is it warmer in summer?
answers: In summer (around June 21 in the north)
The sun is higher and shines longer each day

lessons.title: How to Make a Sun-dial
steps: Outdoors: With a parent, make a simple sundial from cardboard and a pencil and set it in a sunny spot
Parent reads the Teacher's Story for "How to Make a Sun-dial" (p. 915) beforehand and shares the most interesting facts aloud
Nature journal: draw your sundial with hour marks and write one sentence about what you noticed

links.label: Read: How to Make a Sun-dial (p. 915)

questions: What is the part of a sundial that casts the shadow called?
Which way should the gnomon point?
answers: The gnomon
Toward the North Star (true north)

lessons.title: The Moon
steps: Nature walk: Watch the moon every clear night for two weeks and draw its shape each time
Parent previews the background reading on "The Moon" (p. 918) and retells the best parts to the children
Nature journal: draw the moon's shape night by night and write one sentence about what you noticed
questions: Does the moon make its own light?
Why do we always see the same face of the moon?
What are the round holes on the moon called?
answers: No; it reflects sunlight
It turns once each time it goes around the earth
Craters
